    Step 5 – Turn PDFs into page-level “documents”

    Next, we convert each PDF into a list of page-level records. Each record stores:

    • text: page text (as extracted by pypdf).
    • doc_id: short ID from metadata.csv (e.g., strubell2019).
    • title: title of the document.
    • url: original PDF URL.
    • page_num: zero-based page index.
    • page_label: label used inside the PDF (often 1-based).

    Later, we will chunk these pages into smaller overlapping segments for embedding.

    Why we page-chunk first

    We split the PDF into pages before chunking because pages give us a stable, easy-to-interpret unit.
    This helps with:

    • Keeping metadata (doc ID, URL, page labels) tied to the text.
    • Debugging retrieval — it’s much easier to understand what the model saw if we know which page(s) were used.
    • Cleaning text before making smaller overlapping chunks.
    • Flexibility later — once pages are structured, we can try different chunk sizes or strategies without re-extracting the PDF.

    In short: pages first → then chunks keeps the workflow cleaner and easier to reason about.

    PYTHON 

    %pip install -q pypdf

    PYTHON 

    from pypdf import PdfReader

def pdfs_to_page_docs(metadata: pd.DataFrame, pdf_dir: str) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """Load each PDF into a list of page-level dictionaries.

    Each dict has keys: text, doc_id, title, url, page_num, page_label, total_pages.
    """
    page_docs: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []

    for _, row in metadata.iterrows():
        doc_id = str(row["id"]).strip()
        title = str(row.get("title", "")).strip()
        url = str(row.get("url", "")).strip()

        pdf_path = os.path.join(pdf_dir, f"{doc_id}.pdf")
        if not os.path.exists(pdf_path):
            print(f"Missing PDF for {doc_id}, skipping.")
            continue

        try:
            reader = PdfReader(pdf_path)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Failed to read {pdf_path}: {e}")
            continue

        total_pages = len(reader.pages)
        for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
            try:
                text = page.extract_text() or ""
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Failed to extract text from {doc_id} page {i}: {e}")
                text = ""

            text = text.strip()
            if not text:
                # Still keep the page so we know it exists, but mark it as empty
                text = "[[EMPTY PAGE TEXT – see original PDF for tables/figures]]"

            page_docs.append(
                {
                    "text": text,
                    "doc_id": doc_id,
                    "title": title,
                    "url": url,
                    "page_num": i,
                    "page_label": str(i + 1),
                    "total_pages": total_pages,
                }
            )

    return page_docs


page_docs = pdfs_to_page_docs(metadata_df, PDF_DIR)
print(f"Loaded {len(page_docs)} page-level records from {len(metadata_df)} PDFs.")
page_docs[0] if page_docs else None

    Step 6 – Simple, explicit text chunking

    RAG systems typically break documents into chunks so that:

    • Each chunk is long enough to carry meaningful context.
    • No chunk is so long that it blows up the embedding/LLM context window.

    For this workshop we will implement a simple sliding-window chunker that operates on characters:

    • chunk_size_chars: maximum characters per chunk (e.g., 1,000–1,500).
    • chunk_overlap_chars: overlap between consecutive chunks (e.g., 200).

    In your own work, you may wish to plug in more sophisticated semantic chunking methods (e.g., splitting on headings, section titles, or sentence boundaries). For now, we’ll keep the implementation explicit and easy to debug.

    PYTHON 

    def split_text_into_chunks(
    text: str,
    chunk_size_chars: int = 1200,
    chunk_overlap_chars: int = 200,
) -> List[str]:
    """Split `text` into overlapping character-based chunks.

    This is a simple baseline; more advanced versions might:
    - split on sentence boundaries, or
    - merge short paragraphs and respect section headings.
    """
    text = text.strip()
    if not text:
        return []

    chunks: List[str] = []
    start = 0
    text_len = len(text)

    while start < text_len:
        end = min(start + chunk_size_chars, text_len)
        chunk = text[start:end]
        chunks.append(chunk)
        if end == text_len:
            break
        # Move the window forward, keeping some overlap
        start = end - chunk_overlap_chars

    return chunks


def make_chunked_docs(
    page_docs: List[Dict[str, Any]],
    chunk_size_chars: int = 1200,
    chunk_overlap_chars: int = 200,
) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """Turn page-level records into smaller overlapping text chunks.

    Each chunk keeps a pointer back to its document and page metadata.
    """
    chunked: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
    for page in page_docs:
        page_text = page["text"]
        chunks = split_text_into_chunks(
            page_text,
            chunk_size_chars=chunk_size_chars,
            chunk_overlap_chars=chunk_overlap_chars,
        )
        for idx, chunk_text in enumerate(chunks):
            chunked.append(
                {
                    "text": chunk_text,
                    "doc_id": page["doc_id"],
                    "title": page["title"],
                    "url": page["url"],
                    "page_num": page["page_num"],
                    "page_label": page["page_label"],
                    "total_pages": page["total_pages"],
                    "chunk_idx_in_page": idx,
                }
            )
    return chunked

    Chunking is cheap CPU work, but there is no reason to repeat it on every run. We save the chunks locally as data/chunks.jsonl (one JSON record per line) and reload the file if it already exists.

    PYTHON 

    chunks_jsonl_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "chunks.jsonl")

def save_chunked_docs_jsonl(path, chunks):
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for rec in chunks:
            json.dump(rec, f, ensure_ascii=False)
            f.write("\n")


def load_chunked_docs_jsonl(path):
    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return [json.loads(line) for line in f]

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Cached chunking logic
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
if os.path.exists(chunks_jsonl_path):
    print(f"Found existing chunk file: {chunks_jsonl_path}")
    chunked_docs = load_chunked_docs_jsonl(chunks_jsonl_path)
    print("Loaded chunked docs:", len(chunked_docs))
else:
    print("No chunk file found. Running chunking step...")
    chunked_docs = make_chunked_docs(page_docs)
    save_chunked_docs_jsonl(chunks_jsonl_path, chunked_docs)
    print(f"Saved chunked docs to {chunks_jsonl_path}")

# Show first chunk
print("Raw pages:", len(page_docs))
print("Chunked docs:", len(chunked_docs))
chunked_docs[0] if chunked_docs else None

    PYTHON 

    # Upload to YOUR bucket so the Processing Jobs episode (and future runs) can reuse the
# chunks without repeating the unpacking and chunking steps.
print(f"Uploading chunked docs to s3://{bucket_name}/{chunks_key} ...")
s3.upload_file(chunks_jsonl_path, bucket_name, chunks_key)
print("Upload complete.")

    Step 7 – Cost tracking: Bedrock calls carry no tags unless you route them through a profile

    In the SageMaker episodes that follow, we tag every job at launch because tags never propagate from the notebook. Bedrock is stricter still: an on-demand invoke_model or converse call has no tags parameter at all. If you call deepseek.v3-v1:0 or amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 by its model ID, the usage lands in the account’s Bedrock bill as anonymous per-token charges. The notebook’s tags, the bucket’s tags, and the tags you set on anything else are irrelevant to it. On a shared account that means nobody can tell which team spent what.

    The mechanism Bedrock provides for this is an application inference profile: a small, free resource that points at a base model and carries cost allocation tags. You create the profile once, then pass the profile ARN instead of the model ID as modelId in every call. Usage billed through the profile carries the profile’s tags into Cost Explorer. Two details to get right:

    • You need one profile per base model (the profile is model‑specific), so we create one for the generation model and one for the embedding model.
    • Bedrock’s tag format uses lowercase key / value, unlike SageMaker’s Key / Value. The tag names (Name, Project, Purpose) stay the same so the Cost Explorer filters line up across services.

    The helper below reuses a profile if one with the same name already exists, so re‑running the notebook does not create duplicates.

    PYTHON 

    import re

name = "John Doe"        # replace with your name
project = "sinkorswim"   # replace with your challenge name
purpose = "RAG-bedrock"

# Bedrock tags are lowercase key/value (SageMaker jobs use Key/Value)
profile_tags = [
    {"key": "Name", "value": name},
    {"key": "Project", "value": project},
    {"key": "Purpose", "value": purpose},
]

def _slug(text: str) -> str:
    # Profile names allow letters, digits, and single spaces/hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars
    return re.sub(r"[^0-9a-zA-Z]+", "-", text).strip("-")[:30]

def _source_arn(model_id: str) -> str:
    """ARN that the profile should point at.

    Plain model IDs (e.g. 'amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0') map to a foundation-model ARN.
    Cross-region IDs (e.g. 'us.deepseek.v3-v1:0') are system-defined
    inference profiles, so we copy from that profile's ARN instead.
    """
    if model_id.split(".")[0] in {"us", "eu", "apac", "global", "jp", "au"}:
        return bedrock.get_inference_profile(inferenceProfileIdentifier=model_id)["inferenceProfileArn"]
    return bedrock.get_foundation_model(modelIdentifier=model_id)["modelDetails"]["modelArn"]

def get_or_create_inference_profile(base_model_id: str, label: str) -> str:
    """Return the ARN of a tagged application inference profile for base_model_id."""
    profile_name = f"{_slug(project)}-{_slug(name)}-{label}"

    # Reuse an existing profile with this name, if any
    paginator = bedrock.get_paginator("list_inference_profiles")
    for page in paginator.paginate(typeEquals="APPLICATION"):
        for summary in page["inferenceProfileSummaries"]:
            if summary["inferenceProfileName"] == profile_name:
                print(f"Reusing inference profile {profile_name}: {summary['inferenceProfileArn']}")
                return summary["inferenceProfileArn"]

    resp = bedrock.create_inference_profile(
        inferenceProfileName=profile_name,
        description=f"{project} / {name} WattBot RAG ({label}) -> {base_model_id}",
        modelSource={"copyFrom": _source_arn(base_model_id)},
        tags=profile_tags,
    )
    print(f"Created inference profile {profile_name}: {resp['inferenceProfileArn']}")
    return resp["inferenceProfileArn"]

# From here on, these ARNs are what we pass as modelId. The base IDs are never sent to
# the runtime again.
bedrock_model_id = get_or_create_inference_profile(base_generation_model_id, "wattbot-gen")
embedding_model_id_bedrock = get_or_create_inference_profile(base_embedding_model_id, "wattbot-embed")
    Callout

    Permissions and verification

    • The notebook’s execution role needs bedrock:CreateInferenceProfile, bedrock:GetInferenceProfile, bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles, bedrock:GetFoundationModel, and bedrock:TagResource in addition to bedrock:InvokeModel. The InvokeModel permission must cover both the profile ARN and the underlying model ARN, or calls through the profile are denied. If create_inference_profile raises AccessDeniedException, ask the account administrator for these permissions rather than falling back to the raw model ID.
    • You can confirm the routing in the Bedrock console under Inference and Assessment → Cross-region inference → Application inference profiles, or with bedrock.list_inference_profiles(typeEquals="APPLICATION").
    • Tags only become filters in Cost Explorer once the tag keys have been activated as cost allocation tags in the Billing console (an account‑admin, once‑per‑key action; on a shared workshop account the organizers do this). Until then the tags exist on the resource but do not show up on reports.
    • The profile itself has no hourly or storage charge. You only pay per token, exactly as before.
    Challenge

    Who is paying for these tokens?

    List the application inference profiles in the account and find your two. For each, print its name, the model it points at, and its tags (bedrock.list_tags_for_resource takes the profile ARN). Then answer: if a teammate skipped this step and called deepseek.v3-v1:0 by its raw model ID for the rest of the episode, what would Cost Explorer show when the organizers filter the month’s Bedrock spend by Project?

    PYTHON 

    profiles = bedrock.list_inference_profiles(typeEquals="APPLICATION")["inferenceProfileSummaries"]
print(f"{len(profiles)} application inference profiles in this account/region")
for p in profiles:
    if p["inferenceProfileArn"] in {bedrock_model_id, embedding_model_id_bedrock}:
        tags = bedrock.list_tags_for_resource(resourceARN=p["inferenceProfileArn"])["tags"]
        print(p["inferenceProfileName"], "->", [m["modelArn"].split("/")[-1] for m in p["models"]])
        print("   tags:", {t["key"]: t["value"] for t in tags})

    Filtering by Project shows only the usage that went through a tagged profile. The teammate’s calls are still on the bill, under the Bedrock service line for deepseek.v3-v1:0, but with no Project, Name or Purpose value: in the grouped view they fall into the “No tag key: Project” bucket, together with every other untagged call in the account. There is no way to attribute them after the fact; tags are applied when the usage is metered, not later. That is why the base model ID is never passed to the runtime in this episode.

    Step 8 – Embed the chunks with Titan

    Everything the RAG loop needs is now in memory: the chunks, the questions, and a way to resolve a document id to its URL for the ref_url column.

    PYTHON 

    print(f"Chunks: {len(chunked_docs)}")
print(f"Train QAs: {len(train_df)}")
print(f"Metadata rows: {len(metadata_df)}")

docid_to_url = build_docid_to_url(metadata_df)
print(f"docid_to_url has {len(docid_to_url)} entries.")

    Titan Text Embeddings V2 takes one string per invoke_model call and returns a 1,024-dimensional normalized vector. embedding_model_id_bedrock is the ARN of our tagged profile for it, so every call is attributed to our Project/Name/Purpose tags. The embedding loop takes a few minutes for ~3,000 chunks (one HTTPS round trip each); it saves its progress every 500 chunks so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped, and uploads the finished matrix to your bucket.

    PYTHON 

    data_dir = Path(local_data_dir)
emb_save_path = data_dir / "embeddings_bedrock.npy"
emb_partial_path = data_dir / "embeddings_bedrock.partial.npy"

def bedrock_embed_text(text: str, model_id: str = embedding_model_id_bedrock) -> List[float]:
    """Call the Titan embedding model (through our tagged profile) for one string."""
    response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(
        modelId=model_id,
        contentType="application/json",
        accept="application/json",
        body=json.dumps({"inputText": text}),
    )
    response_body = json.loads(response["body"].read())
    embedding = response_body.get("embedding")
    if embedding is None:
        raise ValueError(f"No 'embedding' found in response: {response_body}")
    return embedding


def embed_query(question: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """The retrieval-time half of the pipeline: the same model, one question at a time."""
    return np.asarray(bedrock_embed_text(question), dtype="float32")


def _s3_object_exists(bucket: str, key: str) -> bool:
    try:
        s3.head_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key)
        return True
    except ClientError:
        return False


if emb_save_path.exists():
    print(f"Found existing embeddings at {emb_save_path}. Skipping re-computation.")
    chunk_embeddings = np.load(emb_save_path)
elif _s3_object_exists(bucket_name, embeddings_key):
    s3.download_file(bucket_name, embeddings_key, str(emb_save_path))
    print(f"Downloaded cached embeddings from s3://{bucket_name}/{embeddings_key}")
    chunk_embeddings = np.load(emb_save_path)
else:
    # Resume from a partial save if a previous run was interrupted
    all_embeddings = list(np.load(emb_partial_path)) if emb_partial_path.exists() else []
    start = len(all_embeddings)
    print(f"Computing embeddings via Bedrock from chunk {start} of {len(chunked_docs)}...")

    for idx in range(start, len(chunked_docs)):
        all_embeddings.append(bedrock_embed_text(chunked_docs[idx]["text"]))
        if (idx + 1) % 500 == 0 or idx + 1 == len(chunked_docs):
            np.save(emb_partial_path, np.array(all_embeddings, dtype="float32"))
            print(f"Embedded {idx + 1} / {len(chunked_docs)} chunks (progress saved)")

    chunk_embeddings = np.array(all_embeddings, dtype="float32")
    np.save(emb_save_path, chunk_embeddings)
    emb_partial_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    s3.upload_file(str(emb_save_path), bucket_name, embeddings_key)
    print(f"Saved embeddings to {emb_save_path} and s3://{bucket_name}/{embeddings_key}")

assert chunk_embeddings.shape[0] == len(chunked_docs), "embeddings and chunks are out of step; delete the cached files and rerun"
print("Embeddings shape:", chunk_embeddings.shape)

    Step 9 – Retrieve: cosine similarity over the embedding matrix

    Retrieval is pure NumPy: embed the question with the same model, take the cosine similarity against every chunk, and keep the top k. retrieve_top_k from wattbot_rag.py does that (open the file to see it: it is a normalize-and-matrix-multiply). No vector database is needed for a few thousand chunks; the optional GPU-notebook episode discusses when one becomes worth it.

    PYTHON 

    first_row = train_df.iloc[0]
print("Sample question:", first_row["question"])

test_retrieved = retrieve_top_k(embed_query(first_row["question"]), chunk_embeddings, chunked_docs, k=3)
for r in test_retrieved:
    snippet = r["text"].replace("\n", " ")[:160]
    print(f"- score={r['score']:.3f} | doc_id={r['doc_id']} | page={r['page_label']} | {snippet}...")

    Step 10 – Generate: DeepSeek V3 through the converse API

    Bedrock has two runtime APIs. invoke_model takes a provider-specific request body (which is why the Titan call above builds a {"inputText": ...} body by hand). converse is provider-neutral: a system prompt, a list of messages, and an inferenceConfig, in the same shape for DeepSeek, Claude, Llama and the rest. We use converse for generation so the model is a one-line swap. The response carries the generated text and a usage block with the input and output token counts, which is what Bedrock bills on; we keep every usage block so we can price the run at the end.

    PYTHON 

    bedrock_usage = []   # one {"inputTokens": ..., "outputTokens": ...} per call

def call_bedrock_chat(
    system_prompt: str,
    user_prompt: str,
    max_new_tokens: int = 512,
    model_id: str = bedrock_model_id,   # the tagged profile ARN, never the raw model ID
) -> str:
    """Send one system + user turn to a Bedrock chat model and return the generated text."""
    try:
        response = bedrock_runtime.converse(
            modelId=model_id,
            system=[{"text": system_prompt}],
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": user_prompt}]}],
            inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": max_new_tokens, "temperature": 0},
        )
    except ClientError as e:
        print(f"ERROR calling Bedrock model {model_id}: {e}")
        raise

    bedrock_usage.append(response["usage"])
    # Some models return extra content blocks (e.g. reasoning); keep only the text ones.
    text_blocks = [block["text"] for block in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "text" in block]
    return "\n".join(text_blocks).strip()


print(call_bedrock_chat("You are a concise assistant.", "What is 2 + 2? Answer in one short sentence.", max_new_tokens=32))
print("usage of that call:", bedrock_usage[-1])

    That function has the signature the shared pipeline expects, generate(system_prompt, user_prompt, max_new_tokens) -> str, and embed_query has the other one, embed_query(question) -> vector. Those two callables are the only difference between this episode and the self-hosted ones.

    What the pipeline asks the model

    run_single_qa in wattbot_rag.py makes two calls per question. The first asks for a JSON object in the WattBot submission format, from the retrieved context only; the second, made only when the first produced an answer, asks for a one-to-three-sentence explanation of how the cited material supports it. The system prompt of the first call is the contract that makes the output machine-readable:

    PYTHON 

    print(ANSWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT)

    A question is marked unanswerable (is_blank everywhere, as the competition requires) when the model says so or when the best retrieval score is below retrieval_threshold.

    Step 11 – Run the WattBot evaluation with Bedrock

    Now we can loop over all questions in train_QA.csv, run retrieval + Bedrock generation, and write a wattbot_solutions_bedrock.csv file (locally and to your bucket).

    The Processing Jobs episode reuses this same loop with self-hosted models; the only difference there is that the embedding, answer and explanation phases call local models instead of Bedrock-hosted ones.

    PYTHON 

    results = []

# For quick smoke tests, slice train_df (e.g., train_df.head(5))
for _, row in train_df.iterrows():
    print("#" * 96)
    print(f"QUESTION: {row['question']}")

    out = run_single_qa(
        row=row,
        embed_query=embed_query,
        generate=call_bedrock_chat,
        chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings,
        chunked_docs=chunked_docs,
        docid_to_url=docid_to_url,
        top_k=8,
        retrieval_threshold=0.25,
        verbose=True,
    )

    print(f"ANSWER: {out['answer']}")
    print(f"ref_ids: {out['ref_id']}")
    print(f"EXPLANATION: {out['explanation']}")
    results.append(out)

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)

output_dir = "outputs"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)
output_path = os.path.join(output_dir, "wattbot_solutions_bedrock.csv")
results_df.to_csv(output_path, index=False)
s3.upload_file(output_path, bucket_name, solutions_key)
print(f"Wrote predictions to {output_path} and s3://{bucket_name}/{solutions_key}")

results_df.head()

    Step 12 – Score against the training answers

    WattBot scores each prediction with three components: 0.75 for answer_value (numeric within ±0.1% relative tolerance, categorical exact match), 0.15 for the Jaccard overlap between predicted and ground-truth ref_id sets, and 0.10 for marking unanswerable questions correctly. compute_wattbot_score from wattbot_rag.py implements that, joins on id, and prints the worst-scoring rows so you can see why the pipeline lost points. train_QA.csv has no separate “unanswerable” column, so gt_is_na_col="is_blank" tells the scorer to derive that flag from answer_value == "is_blank" on both sides.

    PYTHON 

    scored_df = compute_wattbot_score(
    train_qa_path=train_qa_path,
    preds_path=output_path,
    gt_is_na_col="is_blank",
    pred_is_na_col="is_blank",
    n_examples=20,
)
    Challenge

    What did that run cost?

    Every converse response carried a usage block, and call_bedrock_chat kept them all in bedrock_usage. Sum the input and output tokens over the evaluation run and price them at the current on-demand rates for DeepSeek V3 on the Bedrock pricing page (fill the two prices in below). Add the embedding step: ~3,000 chunks of 1,200 characters at Titan Text Embeddings V2’s $0.02 per million input tokens. How does the total compare with the overview’s estimate for “the whole WattBot pipeline on Bedrock”, and with one hour of the ml.g6e.xlarge the Processing Jobs episode rents?

    PYTHON 

    price_in_per_m = 0.0    # <-- EDIT ME: DeepSeek V3 on-demand, $ per million input tokens
price_out_per_m = 0.0   # <-- EDIT ME: DeepSeek V3 on-demand, $ per million output tokens

in_tokens = sum(u["inputTokens"] for u in bedrock_usage)
out_tokens = sum(u["outputTokens"] for u in bedrock_usage)
gen_cost = in_tokens / 1e6 * price_in_per_m + out_tokens / 1e6 * price_out_per_m

# Titan bills per input token; ~4 characters per token is a fair estimate for English prose
embed_tokens = sum(len(ch["text"]) for ch in chunked_docs) / 4
embed_cost = embed_tokens / 1e6 * 0.02

print(f"{len(bedrock_usage)} generation calls: {in_tokens:,} input + {out_tokens:,} output tokens -> ${gen_cost:.3f}")
print(f"~{embed_tokens:,.0f} embedding tokens -> ${embed_cost:.3f}")
print(f"Total ~${gen_cost + embed_cost:.2f}; one hour of ml.g6e.xlarge is $2.61")

    With ~40 questions, two calls each and ~3,000-token prompts, the run is on the order of 250K input and 20K output tokens: cents, not dollars, at any price in DeepSeek V3’s class, plus about two cents of embeddings. That matches the overview’s “well under $1” for the whole pipeline, and it is a small fraction of a single GPU-hour.

    Wrap‑up: Bedrock versus GPU‑based runs

    You now have a complete WattBot evaluation running on Bedrock, with per‑token billing and nothing left running. The Processing Jobs episode reruns the same evaluation on a self‑hosted model, and the optional GPU-notebook episode does it once more interactively, so by the end you will have three versions to compare:

    1. Bedrock (this episode) using hosted embedding and generation models with per‑token billing.
    2. SageMaker Processing job running an open‑source model in batch with on-demand compute.
    3. Notebook GPU instance (optional) using the same locally loaded open‑source model.

    When deciding between these options in practice:

    • Use Bedrock or other hosted APIs when:
      • You want to try the latest frontier models quickly.
      • You only need to run a modest number of questions, or you are still prototyping.
      • You prefer a simple, token‑based cost model and don’t want to manage GPU capacity.
    • Use self‑hosted models on GPU instances when:
      • You need a specific open-weight model that the catalog does not carry.
      • You expect to run large batches repeatedly (e.g., many thousands of questions).
      • You want tight control over which architectures/checkpoints you run or fine‑tune.
      • You already have institutional access to cost‑effective on‑prem or cloud GPUs.

    The core RAG evaluation logic stays identical across all three episodes, which is the main takeaway: once you have a clean retrieval + normalization pipeline (like WattBot’s, in wattbot_rag.py), swapping out the generator is mostly a matter of re‑implementing embed_query and generate for each compute option you care about.

    Concluding remarks: Bedrock models are one piece of the RAG puzzle

    In this episode we used Bedrock-hosted models for both embedding and generation. Larger, higher-quality models can definitely help a ton — especially on messy real-world questions — but it’s important to remember that they are still just one component in your RAG system.

    • Bigger or newer models do not magically fix weak retrieval. If your chunks are poorly aligned with the questions, a very strong LLM will still struggle.
    • Most of the long‑term accuracy gains in RAG systems come from the plumbing around the LLMs, including:
      • smarter / semantic chunking strategies
      • good metadata and filtering
      • reranking or multi‑stage retrieval
      • domain‑specific heuristics and post‑processing
    • Cost and latency live in tension with quality. Larger models (or higher token budgets) often improve answers, but at the cost of more inference time and higher per‑request spend. Bedrock makes it easier to experiment with that tradeoff by switching models without rewriting your pipeline.

    As you adapt this notebook to your own projects, treat the LLM choice as one tunable component in a larger system. Iterating on chunking, indexing, and retrieval policies will almost always give you more headroom than swapping between already-good models.

    Key Points
    • A complete RAG pipeline on AWS needs no GPU: a CPU notebook plus Bedrock-hosted embedding and generation models is enough.
    • Corpus preparation (unpacking the staged PDFs, page extraction, chunking) is cheap CPU work; cache chunks.jsonl on S3 so later episodes and runs can reuse it.
    • Bedrock calls carry no tags; route them through a tagged application inference profile or the spend is anonymous on the bill.
    • converse is the provider-neutral way to call a chat model on Bedrock; its usage block is what you are billed on. DeepSeek V3 is the generator here, and any catalog model is a one-line swap.
    • Bedrock bills per token and leaves nothing running between calls, which is why it is the default route for RAG inference.
    • The model is one tunable component; most accuracy gains come from chunking, retrieval, and post-processing.

    Content from RAG with Processing Jobs

    Last updated on 2026-10-19 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 50 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • When does a RAG pipeline need a self-hosted, open-weight model instead of Bedrock, and what is the safest way to rent the GPU for it?
    • How do we run the embedding and generation steps of the WattBot pipeline as SageMaker Processing jobs that end on their own?
    • How do we pass data in and out of a job through S3, and tag the job so its cost is traceable?

    Objectives

    • Explain why Bedrock’s catalog is not enough when you need a specific open-weight model, and why a Processing job is the default way to self-host one for batch work.
    • Launch a GPU Processing job that embeds the cached WattBot chunks with a self-hosted embedding model and writes the vectors to S3.
    • Launch a second Processing job that serves Qwen3.8-27B (an open-weight model Bedrock does not carry) with vLLM and runs the full RAG loop over the training questions.
    • Read a job’s inputs, outputs, arguments and runtime cap, and relate its duration to what it cost.
    • Score the batch predictions with the WattBot metric and compare against the Bedrock run.

    When Bedrock does not have your model

    The Bedrock episode is the default for RAG: per-token billing, nothing left running, two API calls. Bedrock’s catalog is curated, though. It carries Amazon’s models, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, and a few others, and within a family only some sizes, usually a generation behind: for Qwen, the serverless lineup is still the Qwen3 series. Hugging Face hosts well over a million open-weight checkpoints. The one you want (the newest release, a specific size, a fine-tune for scientific text, a model a paper just published) is usually not on Bedrock, and often never will be.

    When that happens you host the model yourself on a GPU you rent, and the question becomes how. There are three ways to rent a GPU on SageMaker:

    Bills Stops when Best for
    GPU notebook instance by the hour from start to stop you stop it interactive debugging, prototyping at the keyboard
    Processing or training job by the second while the job runs the script ends, or max_runtime_in_seconds batch work: embed a corpus, answer a list of questions, train
    Inference endpoint by the hour while deployed you delete it serving a model to an application with steady traffic

    For research RAG, almost all the work is batch: embed everything once, answer a list of questions, score them. That is a job, and a job is the one option that cannot be forgotten. This episode runs the WattBot pipeline that way. The notebook itself is a small CPU instance and never touches the model; it stages data, launches two GPU jobs, and reads the results back.

    The generator is Qwen3.8-27B, a 27-billion-parameter open-weight model (Apache 2.0, released August 2026) that is not on Bedrock. Its weights are served in FP8 through vLLM: inference needs no gradients, so the weights are the memory cost, and 27B parameters at one byte each is about 27 GB, which fits one 48 GB GPU (ml.g6e.xlarge) with room for the KV cache. In bf16 the same model is 54 GB and would need a multi-GPU instance for no gain in output quality. (The fine-tuning episode has the full memory arithmetic; the short version is that inference runs on reduced-precision weights and training cannot.)

    Callout

    What this episode costs

    Job Instance $/h Expected duration Cost
    Embed ~3,000 chunks ml.g5.xlarge (A10G, 24 GB) $1.41 ~8 min incl. startup ~$0.20
    RAG over the training questions with Qwen3.8-27B ml.g6e.xlarge (L40S, 48 GB) $2.61 ~30 min: 5 startup, ~5 installing vLLM, ~5 downloading 27 GB of weights, the rest generating ~$1.30
    Controller notebook ml.t3.medium $0.05 2 h $0.10

    About $1.60 for the episode, and the GPUs are off the moment each script ends. Both jobs carry max_runtime_in_seconds, so a hung job costs at most the cap. Compare the same pipeline on a GPU notebook instance (the optional GPU-notebook episode at the end of the lesson): the hardware is the same, but the meter runs until someone stops it, and a forgotten ml.g6e.xlarge is $63 a day.

    The trade-off is latency. A job takes minutes to start, so this pattern is for batch questions, not a chatbot. For interactive use, Bedrock answers in seconds; for interactive use of a model Bedrock does not have, an inference endpoint does, at an hourly rate you have to remember to turn off.

    In this episode we will:

    • Reuse the chunks cached in your bucket by the Bedrock episode and the inputs in the shared bucket.
    • Run two short-lived GPU Processing jobs: one computes embeddings for all chunks; the second serves Qwen3.8-27B with vLLM and runs the full RAG loop (retrieval + generation) over all training questions.
    • Score the result and compare it with the Bedrock run.

    Setup

    The scripts

    Jobs run in containers, so the code they execute has to be shipped with the job: a Processing job cannot import functions defined in this notebook. The lesson repository has the three files we need as standalone scripts. Clone it:

    PYTHON 

    !test -d ML_with_AWS_SageMaker || git clone https://github.com/carpentries-incubator/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker.git
    • scripts/embedding_inference.py: generic embedding script (JSONL with a text field in, embeddings.npy out).
    • scripts/wattbot_rag_batch.py: the WattBot RAG loop as a batch job: loads the inputs, serves Qwen with vLLM, writes wattbot_solutions.csv.
    • scripts/wattbot_rag.py: the shared pipeline logic (retrieval, prompts, answer parsing, run_single_qa, the scorer) that the Bedrock episode imported too. The batch script imports it, so it ships with the job; the notebook imports it for scoring.

    Each job gets its own source directory, because the two jobs need different Python packages and SageMaker installs whatever requirements.txt it finds next to the script. code_embed/ holds the embedding job, code_rag/ the RAG job, and a copy of wattbot_rag.py sits next to the notebook for the scoring step at the end.

    PYTHON 

    !mkdir -p code_embed code_rag
!cp ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/embedding_inference.py code_embed/
!cp ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag_batch.py ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag.py code_rag/
!cp ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag.py .
!ls code_embed code_rag

    Next, set up the AWS SDK, SageMaker session, and bucket names.

    PYTHON

import json

import boto3
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import sagemaker
from sagemaker import get_execution_role
from sagemaker.huggingface import HuggingFaceProcessor
from sagemaker.processing import ProcessingInput, ProcessingOutput

session = sagemaker.Session()
region = session.boto_region_name
role = get_execution_role()

shared_bucket = "ml-marathon-shared"   # <-- EDIT ME: read-only inputs, from your instructor
bucket_name = "sinkorswim-doejohn"     # <-- EDIT ME: your own bucket (chunks in, outputs out)
s3_client = boto3.client("s3", region_name=region)

local_data_dir = "./data"
os.makedirs(local_data_dir, exist_ok=True)

print("Region:", region)
print("Role:", role)
print("Bucket:", bucket_name)

    Step 1 – Check the inputs

    The jobs read three files from S3: train_QA.csv and metadata.csv from the shared bucket, and chunks.jsonl from your bucket, where the Bedrock episode cached it. The PDFs themselves are not needed again: chunking was done once, and the jobs work from the chunks. We download the three files to the notebook only to confirm they exist and to look at them; the jobs fetch their own copies from S3.

    PYTHON 

    train_qa_key = "wattbot/train_QA.csv"
metadata_key = "wattbot/metadata.csv"
chunks_s3_key = "wattbot/chunks.jsonl"

train_qa_s3 = f"s3://{shared_bucket}/{train_qa_key}"
metadata_s3 = f"s3://{shared_bucket}/{metadata_key}"
chunks_s3_uri = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{chunks_s3_key}"

def smart_read_csv(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    try:
        return pd.read_csv(path)
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        return pd.read_csv(path, encoding="latin-1")

train_qa_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "train_QA.csv")
metadata_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "metadata.csv")
local_chunks_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "chunks.jsonl")

if not os.path.exists(train_qa_path):
    s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, train_qa_key, train_qa_path)
if not os.path.exists(metadata_path):
    s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, metadata_key, metadata_path)
if not os.path.exists(local_chunks_path):
    s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, chunks_s3_key, local_chunks_path)   # written by the Bedrock episode

train_df = smart_read_csv(train_qa_path)
metadata_df = smart_read_csv(metadata_path)
with open(local_chunks_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    chunked_docs = [json.loads(line) for line in f]

print("Train QAs:", len(train_df))
print("Metadata rows:", len(metadata_df))
print("Chunks:", len(chunked_docs), "from", chunks_s3_uri)
train_df.head(3)

    If the last download fails with NoSuchKey, go back to the Bedrock episode and run its chunking step; this episode starts from its output.

    Step 2 – Processing Job 1: embed all chunks on a GPU

    Now we launch a short-lived Hugging Face Processing job that:

    1. Downloads chunks.jsonl from S3.
    2. Loads thenlper/gte-large from Hugging Face.
    3. Encodes each chunk into an embedding vector.
    4. Saves the full matrix as embeddings.npy back to S3.

    We use the same embedding_inference.py script across projects; here it expects a JSONL file with a text field.

    Requirements

    The Hugging Face container has transformers and PyTorch but not sentence-transformers. A requirements.txt in the job’s source_dir is installed before the script runs. The RAG job’s requirements are different (vLLM, plus sentence-transformers for the query embedder), which is why it has its own directory.

    PYTHON 

    with open("code_embed/requirements.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("sentence-transformers\n")

with open("code_rag/requirements.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(["vllm>=0.17", "sentence-transformers"]) + "\n")   # 0.17+ is needed for Qwen3.8

print("code_embed:", os.listdir("code_embed"))
print("code_rag:  ", os.listdir("code_rag"))
    Callout

    The RAG job’s pip install is part of its bill

    vLLM ships its own CUDA kernels and pins its own PyTorch, so pip install vllm in the RAG job pulls several gigabytes and replaces the container’s torch and transformers with the versions it wants. That is normal (the container is thrown away when the job ends) but it takes about 5 of the job’s ~30 minutes, on a GPU instance that is billing the whole time: roughly 20 cents per run. For a job you launch often, bake the install into a custom container image instead; for a job you launch twice in a workshop, paying for the install is cheaper than building the image.

    Cost tracking: tag every job

    Tags do not propagate in AWS. The tags you put on your notebook instance cover the notebook’s hourly cost and nothing else. Each Processing job below launches its own GPU instance, which is a separate billable resource with no tags unless we pass them at launch, exactly as we did for training and tuning jobs earlier in the workshop. An untagged job shows up in Cost Explorer as anonymous SageMaker spend that nobody can attribute to a team.

    Define the tags once and pass tags=job_tags to every HuggingFaceProcessor you create. Use a distinct Purpose per job so you can tell the embedding job from the batch RAG job on the bill.

    PYTHON 

    name = "John Doe"        # replace with your name
project = "sinkorswim"   # replace with your challenge name

def make_job_tags(purpose: str):
    return [
        {"Key": "Name", "Value": name},
        {"Key": "Project", "Value": project},
        {"Key": "Purpose", "Value": purpose},
    ]

    Launch the embedding job

    PYTHON 

    embedding_model_id = "thenlper/gte-large"

emb_output_prefix = "wattbot/embeddings"
emb_output_path = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{emb_output_prefix}/"

embedding_processor = HuggingFaceProcessor(
    base_job_name="WattBot-embed-gte-large",
    role=role,
    tags=make_job_tags("RAG-embed"),   # tags are per job; nothing is inherited from the notebook
    instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge",
    instance_count=1,
    transformers_version="4.56",
    pytorch_version="2.8",
    py_version="py312",
    sagemaker_session=session,
    max_runtime_in_seconds=2 * 60 * 60,   # backstop: the estimate is 8 minutes
)

embedding_processor.run(
    code="embedding_inference.py",
    source_dir="code_embed/",
    inputs=[
        ProcessingInput(
            source=chunks_s3_uri,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input",
        )
    ],
    outputs=[
        ProcessingOutput(
            output_name="embeddings",
            source="/opt/ml/processing/output",
            destination=emb_output_path,
        )
    ],
    arguments=[
        "--model_id", embedding_model_id,
        "--input_filename", "chunks.jsonl",
        "--text_key", "text",
        "--input_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/input",
        "--output_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/output",
    ],
)

print("Embedding job complete.")

    Check on the running job in the AWS Console

    To view the job running from the AWS Console, you can visit SageMaker AI, and then find the “Data Preparation” dropdown menu on the left side panel. Click that to find “Processing jobs”. If you’re in us-east-1, the following link should bring you there: https://us-east-1.console.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/home?region=us-east-1#/processing-jobs

    It takes ~5-8 minutes in total for the job to complete, most of it provisioning the instance and installing the requirements. This is the downside of launching jobs, but the good news is that we only need to launch one embedding job for our RAG pipeline. This strategy also ensures we’re only paying for the GPU while the job runs.

    Sanity-check the embeddings locally

    We can download embeddings.npy back into the notebook and inspect its shape to confirm the job ran successfully.

    PYTHON 

    local_embeddings_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "embeddings.npy")
embeddings_key = f"{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy"

s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, embeddings_key, local_embeddings_path)
chunk_embeddings = np.load(local_embeddings_path)

print("Embeddings shape:", chunk_embeddings.shape, "for", len(chunked_docs), "chunks")

    Step 3 – Processing Job 2: full WattBot RAG over all questions

    For the second job, we pass four inputs:

    • chunks.jsonl – serialized chunks (your bucket)
    • embeddings.npy – precomputed chunk embeddings (your bucket, written by Job 1)
    • train_QA.csv – training questions (shared bucket)
    • metadata.csv – to resolve ref_id → URL (shared bucket)

    The script wattbot_rag_batch.py is short, because the pipeline lives in scripts/wattbot_rag.py, the same module the Bedrock episode imported:

    • retrieve_top_k: cosine similarity over the embedding matrix
    • run_single_qa: retrieval, the answer call, the hybrid unanswerable rule (retrieval threshold OR the model’s own is_blank), the explanation call
    • compute_wattbot_score: the metric we use at the end

    What the batch script adds is the two model callables: embed_query wraps the same gte-large sentence-transformer the embedding job used (the question has to be embedded with the same model as the chunks), and generate wraps a vLLM engine serving Qwen3.8-27B with thinking mode off. The job writes wattbot_solutions.csv in the WattBot submission format.

    PYTHON 

    emb_output_s3 = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy"

print("chunks:    ", chunks_s3_uri)
print("embeddings:", emb_output_s3)
print("train_QA:  ", train_qa_s3)
print("metadata:  ", metadata_s3)

    Two settings on this processor matter more than on the embedding job. volume_size_in_gb=60 attaches a 60 GB volume to the instance, mounted under /opt/ml/processing; the container’s own root disk is small, so the 27 GB of model weights (and vLLM’s install) must not land there. env={"HF_HOME": ...} points Hugging Face’s download cache at that volume, which is where the weights go.

    PYTHON 

    rag_output_prefix = "wattbot/solutions"
rag_output_path = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{rag_output_prefix}/"

generation_model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8"   # open-weight, not on Bedrock; ~27 GB in FP8

rag_processor = HuggingFaceProcessor(
    base_job_name="WattBot-rag-batch",
    role=role,
    tags=make_job_tags("RAG-batch"),   # separate job, separate tags
    instance_type="ml.g6e.xlarge",     # 1 x L40S, 48 GB: holds the FP8 27B model plus KV cache
    instance_count=1,
    volume_size_in_gb=60,              # 27 GB of weights + vLLM install; mounted at /opt/ml/processing
    env={"HF_HOME": "/opt/ml/processing/hf_cache"},   # put the weight download on that volume
    transformers_version="4.56",
    pytorch_version="2.8",
    py_version="py312",
    sagemaker_session=session,
    max_runtime_in_seconds=2 * 60 * 60,   # cap: the estimate is 30 minutes
)

rag_processor.run(
    code="wattbot_rag_batch.py",
    source_dir="code_rag/",            # wattbot_rag_batch.py + wattbot_rag.py + requirements.txt
    inputs=[
        ProcessingInput(
            source=chunks_s3_uri,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/chunks",
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=emb_output_s3,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/embeddings",
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=train_qa_s3,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/train",
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=metadata_s3,
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/metadata",
        ),
    ],
    outputs=[
        ProcessingOutput(
            output_name="solutions",
            source="/opt/ml/processing/output",
            destination=rag_output_path,
        )
    ],
    arguments=[
        "--input_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/input",
        "--output_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/output",
        "--embedding_model_id", embedding_model_id,
        "--qwen_model_id", generation_model_id,
        "--top_k", "8",
        "--retrieval_threshold", "0.25",
    ],
)

print("RAG batch job complete.")

    While it runs, open the job’s CloudWatch log from the console page above. You will see, in order: pip installing vLLM, the weight download (27 GB in shards), vLLM loading the model and reporting how much GPU memory it reserved, then one line per question. The whole job is the 30 minutes in the cost callout; the generation is the last third of it.

    Step 4 – Download predictions and evaluate

    Finally, we download wattbot_solutions.csv from S3, inspect a few rows, and compute the WattBot score against train_QA.csv with the same compute_wattbot_score the Bedrock episode used.

    PYTHON 

    solutions_key = f"{rag_output_prefix}/wattbot_solutions.csv"
local_solutions_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "wattbot_solutions.csv")

s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, solutions_key, local_solutions_path)
solutions_df = pd.read_csv(local_solutions_path)
solutions_df.head()

    PYTHON 

    from wattbot_rag import compute_wattbot_score

results_df = compute_wattbot_score(
    train_qa_path=train_qa_path,
    preds_path=local_solutions_path,
    gt_is_na_col="is_blank",
    pred_is_na_col="is_blank",
    n_examples=10,
)

    Compare the overall score with the Bedrock run. The retrieval logic, prompts and scoring are identical, so any difference is the two models: gte-large versus Titan for retrieval, Qwen3.8-27B versus DeepSeek V3 for generation.

    Challenge

    What did the two jobs cost?

    Ask SageMaker what it recorded for each job: session.sagemaker_client.describe_processing_job(ProcessingJobName=...) returns CreationTime, ProcessingStartTime and ProcessingEndTime. The job names are embedding_processor.latest_job.job_name and rag_processor.latest_job.job_name. For each job, compute the minutes between creation and start (provisioning, before the instance is billed) and between start and end (the billed window), and price the billed window at $1.41/h for the ml.g5.xlarge and $2.61/h for the ml.g6e.xlarge. Then, from the RAG job’s CloudWatch log timestamps, estimate how much of its billed window was setup (pip install and weight download) and how much was generation. How does the total compare with the cost callout, and with the Bedrock run?

    PYTHON 

    def job_cost(job_name: str, price_per_hour: float):
    d = session.sagemaker_client.describe_processing_job(ProcessingJobName=job_name)
    provisioning = (d["ProcessingStartTime"] - d["CreationTime"]).total_seconds() / 60
    billed = (d["ProcessingEndTime"] - d["ProcessingStartTime"]).total_seconds() / 60
    cost = billed / 60 * price_per_hour
    print(f"{job_name}: {d['ProcessingJobStatus']}")
    print(f"  provisioning (not billed): {provisioning:.1f} min")
    print(f"  billed window:             {billed:.1f} min at ${price_per_hour}/h = ${cost:.2f}")
    return cost

total = job_cost(embedding_processor.latest_job.job_name, 1.41)
total += job_cost(rag_processor.latest_job.job_name, 2.61)
print(f"GPU total for the episode: ${total:.2f}")

    Typical numbers: the embedding job bills 5-6 minutes (about $0.13), the RAG job 22-28 minutes (about $1.00-$1.20), so roughly $1.20-$1.40 of GPU time against the callout’s $1.50. In the RAG job’s log, the first 10-12 minutes of the billed window are pip and the download; the model loads for another minute or two; the remaining ~10 minutes are the questions, about 15 seconds each for two generation calls. So well over half of what you paid for was setup, which is the argument for a custom container (skip the pip) and for keeping an HF_HOME cache on S3 (skip the download) once a job is run routinely. The Bedrock run of the same questions cost cents, and the self-hosted route is only justified here because the model is not in the catalog.

    Challenge

    The runtime cap

    Both processors set max_runtime_in_seconds=2 * 60 * 60. Predict what would happen if the RAG job were launched with max_runtime_in_seconds=600 instead: what does the job status become, what is in the output prefix, and what did it cost? Then compute the most a hung job can bill under each job’s actual cap, and compare it with the cost of an ml.g6e.xlarge notebook instance left running over a weekend (64 hours).

    With a 600-second cap the RAG job is killed by SageMaker ten minutes after ProcessingStartTime, while it is still installing vLLM or downloading the weights. The status becomes Stopped (the failure reason reads MaxRuntimeExceeded), the output prefix is empty because the script never reached the point of writing wattbot_solutions.csv, and the bill is the full 600 seconds: 600 / 3600 × $2.61 ≈ $0.44 for nothing. A cap has to leave room for the setup that precedes the work, which is why ours is four times the 30-minute estimate rather than ten percent over it.

    Under the caps we set, the worst case for a job that hangs (a stuck download, a model that never finishes loading) is 2 h × $1.41 = $2.82 for the embedding job and 2 h × $2.61 = $5.22 for the RAG job. A ml.g6e.xlarge notebook instance forgotten over a weekend is 64 h × $2.61 = $167, and nothing caps it. That is the difference between a job and an instance: the job’s worst case is a number you chose before you launched it.

    Key Points
    • Bedrock’s catalog is curated and lags releases; when you need a specific open-weight model you rent a GPU and serve it yourself.
    • Of the ways to rent a GPU, a Processing job is the one that cannot be forgotten: it bills while the script runs and ends on its own, with max_runtime_in_seconds as the backstop. Use it for batch work; use Bedrock or an endpoint when you need answers in seconds.
    • Inference runs on reduced-precision weights: Qwen3.8-27B in FP8 is ~27 GB and fits one 48 GB GPU; bf16 would need two.
    • A job’s inputs and outputs are S3 prefixes mounted into the container; the notebook only stages files and reads results, so it stays a cheap CPU instance.
    • The pipeline logic (wattbot_rag.py) ships with the job unchanged from the Bedrock episode; only the two model callables differ.
    • Tags do not propagate from the notebook: every job gets its own tags=.

    Content from Fine-tuning a Vision-Language Model with Training Jobs

    Last updated on 2026-10-19 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 180 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • When is fine-tuning worth it, and how is it different from RAG or prompting?
    • Why does fine-tuning cost anywhere from a dollar to tens of thousands, and how do I estimate where my run falls before I launch it?
    • How do I run a GPU fine-tune as a SageMaker training job so the meter stops the moment it finishes?
    • How do I measure whether the fine-tune helped?

    Objectives

    • Explain what drives the cost of a fine-tuning run (model size × tokens × epochs × number of attempts) and why the same three habits apply at $1 and at $10,000: a time cap, a small first run, and an estimate written down before launch.
    • Launch a LoRA fine-tune of a 3B vision-language model (CHURRO-3B) as a HuggingFace training job on a single 24 GB GPU, with tags, a unique job name and a max_run cap.
    • Read a job’s billable time and compare it to the estimate.
    • Compare the base model and the fine-tuned model on held-out pages using the competition’s own character error rate (CER).
    • Know how to scale the same job up to the full dataset (homework) and to multi-GPU instances for larger models.

    Why a fine-tuning episode

    Everything so far in the RAG episodes left the model’s weights alone. Fine-tuning changes them, and that puts it in a different class of workload:

    • It needs a GPU for the whole run, not just for inference calls.
    • It is iterative. Nobody gets the learning rate, the image resolution or the data split right the first time, so the first run is never the last.
    • The cost of a run depends on things that are easy to get wrong by 10x: model size, epochs, image resolution, instance type, and whether the instance is still running after you stopped paying attention.

    That combination is why fine-tuning is where research teams see surprise bills. Done carefully, it is also where the largest gains are: the Badger Scribe organizers report that LoRA on ~100 pages takes a small open model from 0.23 to 0.06 CER on survey notebooks in about a GPU-hour. This episode is about getting that kind of gain for a few dollars, and about knowing in advance when a run is going to cost a few thousand instead.

    The task: Badger Scribe

    Badger Scribe is a Kaggle challenge built from UW Digital Collections material: 19th-century surveyors’ field notebooks, craftsmen’s account books, and German immigrant letters in Kurrent script. Given a page image, produce a verbatim transcription. The score is character error rate (CER): edits per reference character, lower is better.

    This lesson uses the German letters, the Anna Seifert correspondence held by the Max Kade Institute: 191 letters and postcards written in Kurrent between 1932 and 1942 by one woman to her son, transcribed by the Institute’s Kurrent Transcription Group. It is the part of the competition data where every label was produced by a person, and it is most of the hidden test set.

    split pages documents label source
    train 295 4 letter bundles all human-transcribed, ~620 characters per page
    test 141 5 other letter bundles labels held by Kaggle

    Small is the point. 295 labelled pages is a realistic amount of data for a library or a lab to have, and it is enough to move a model that was pre-trained on the right kind of material. Kurrent is also a genuinely different script from modern German cursive, so this is a case where the model has to learn something, not just adjust its style.

    We will fine-tune CHURRO-3B, a 3-billion-parameter open-weight vision-language model from Stanford that was itself fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL-3B on roughly 100,000 pages of historical documents in 46 language clusters. It already reads old handwriting better than its base model does; we are teaching it these hands and these transcription conventions.

    Callout

    Fine-tune, RAG, or prompt?

    Ask what the model is missing. If it lacks facts (your documents, your data), retrieval gives it those at inference time and no training is needed. If it lacks a skill or a style (reading Kurrent, following your lab’s labelling conventions, producing output in a strict format), you need to change the weights, and that is fine-tuning. Badger Scribe is squarely the second case: no amount of context will teach a model what a Kurrent “e” looks like.

    Full fine-tuning updates all 3 billion weights and needs several times the model’s size in GPU memory for optimizer state. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the model and trains a few million extra parameters in small matrices bolted onto the attention and MLP layers. The adapter is ~100 MB, trains on a single 24 GB GPU, and recovers most of the gain of a full fine-tune for a task like this. We use LoRA.

    Step 0: Estimate the cost before you launch anything

    Before launching a fine-tune, write down what it should cost. If the bill is 3x your number, something is wrong, and you want to know on the first run, not the fiftieth.

    What fine-tuning costs, from one dollar to ten thousand

    The cost of a run is GPU-hours × the hourly rate, and GPU-hours scale with model size × tokens seen × epochs, multiplied by how many runs you do before one works. Our class run sits at the very bottom of that curve. The rows below use current SageMaker on-demand prices in us-east-1 (AWS price list, October 2026):

    Run Hardware GPU-hours Cost
    This episode: 3B, LoRA, 120 Kurrent pages × 2 epochs 1 × A10G (ml.g5.xlarge, $1.41/h), ~25 min 0.4 ~$0.60
    Homework: 3B, LoRA, all 251 training pages × 2 epochs 1 × A10G, ~45 min 0.75 ~$1.05
    7B full fine-tune, 50k documents × 3 epochs (the challenge below) 8 × A100 (ml.p4d.24xlarge, $25.25/h), ~6 h 45 ~$140
    70B LoRA, one day 8 × A100, 24 h 192 ~$600
    CHURRO-3B itself: full fine-tune, 100k pages, 5 epochs 32 × H100 for ~25 h (4 × ml.p5.48xlarge, $63.30/h) 800 ~$6,300
    70B full fine-tune, two days 4 × ml.p5.48xlarge, 48 h 1,536 ~$12,000
    Any row above × a 10-run hyperparameter sweep × 10

    Two rows to note. The CHURRO row is the model you are about to fine-tune: Stanford spent on the order of 800 H100-hours making it, and you get the benefit for sixty cents because you are adapting it, not retraining it. Starting from a model that already knows most of the task is the largest cost saving available, and it is decided before any GPU is involved. The sweep row: a first run is rarely the last, so a “$140 fine-tune” is usually a $700 to $1,400 project. That is the number that surprises research groups. (The 7B row is worked out in the challenge below; the 70B rows are rule-of-thumb magnitudes; the CHURRO figures come from a published review of the paper.)

    The habits in this episode are cheap practice at sixty cents a run. At $140 a run they are the difference between a project and a budget incident.

    Back of the envelope: will it fit, and how long will it take?

    Two rules of thumb answer most of the question before you touch a console. They are good to within a factor of two, which is what you need to tell a $5 run from a $500 one.

    1. Memory: will it fit on the GPU? Count bytes per parameter for what you are doing, multiply by the parameter count, then add a few GB for activations (more for long sequences and big batches).

    What you are doing Bytes per parameter Why 3B 7B 27B 70B
    Inference, 4-bit weights 0.5 weights only 1.5 GB 3.5 GB 14 GB 35 GB
    Inference, FP8 1 weights only 3 GB 7 GB 27 GB 70 GB
    Inference, bf16 2 weights only 6 GB 14 GB 54 GB 140 GB
    LoRA fine-tune ~2.5 frozen bf16 weights + a small adapter with its gradients and optimizer + activations 8 GB 18 GB 68 GB 175 GB
    Full fine-tune, mixed precision 16 bf16 weights 2 + bf16 gradients 2 + fp32 master weights 4 + Adam’s two moments 8 48 GB 112 GB 430 GB 1.1 TB

    Note the jump from the inference rows to the training rows. Training cannot run on quantized weights the way inference can: gradient updates are tiny numbers that vanish in 8-bit or 4-bit precision, so every trainable parameter keeps a full-precision master copy plus two Adam moments, 16 bytes against 2. That is why a 7B model you can run on a 24 GB GPU needs 112 GB plus activations to fully fine-tune, which means several GPUs with the model sharded across them. LoRA sidesteps it by freezing the model and training a few million adapter parameters, which is why this episode fits on one 24 GB card.

    2. Time: how many GPU-hours? Training compute is roughly proportional to parameters × tokens seen:

    tokens      = examples × tokens per example × epochs
FLOPs       ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens      (full fine-tune)
            ≈ 4 × parameters × tokens      (LoRA: no weight gradients for the frozen base)
GPU-seconds = FLOPs / (GPU peak bf16 FLOPS × utilization)

    Utilization is the number people forget. A GPU running one page at a time with gradient checkpointing manages 20–30% of its peak; a well-tuned multi-GPU job reaches 40–50%. Use 25% unless you have measured otherwise, and add ~50% to the FLOPs when gradient checkpointing is on, because it recomputes the forward pass during the backward pass. Both corrections sit inside the factor of two the rule promises. Then cost = GPU-hours × hourly rate + the fixed startup overhead per job (~10 minutes here).

    Worked for the class run: 120 pages × ~1,600 tokens (1,300 visual + 300 text) × 2 epochs = 384k tokens. LoRA on a 3.75B model (3B language model plus the vision tower): 4 × 3.75e9 × 3.84e5 ≈ 5.8e15 FLOPs. An A10G peaks at about 70 TFLOPS in bf16; at 25% utilization that is 17 TFLOPS, so about 340 seconds, call it 6 minutes. The “~10 min” in the table below adds the image preprocessing on four vCPUs and the checkpointing overhead. Same arithmetic, same answer within the factor of two.

    More GPUs do not make it cheaper. GPU-hours are the cost; spreading them across eight GPUs changes the wall-clock time, not the bill, and only helps if the job is large enough to keep all eight busy. You add GPUs when the memory row above says one GPU cannot hold the job, not to save money.

    Challenge

    Estimate a run you have not launched

    A lab wants to fully fine-tune a 7B model on 50,000 documents of ~2,000 tokens for 3 epochs. They are choosing between ml.p4d.24xlarge (8 × A100 40 GB, $25.25/h, ~312 TFLOPS bf16 per GPU) and renting a single ml.g5.xlarge. Using the two rules: does it fit on the g5? How many GPU-hours on the p4d, and what does one run cost? What does a realistic project cost?

    It does not fit on the g5: full fine-tuning a 7B model needs ~112 GB plus activations, and the g5 has 24 GB. On the p4d the 8 × 40 GB = 320 GB holds it with the model sharded.

    Tokens: 50,000 × 2,000 × 3 = 3 × 10^8. FLOPs: 6 × 7 × 10^9 × 3 × 10^8 ≈ 1.26 × 10^19. Per GPU at 312 TFLOPS × 25% utilization = 78 TFLOPS: 1.26 × 10^19 / 7.8 × 10^13 ≈ 1.6 × 10^5 GPU-seconds ≈ 45 GPU-hours, which is about 6 hours of wall-clock on 8 GPUs, about $140 for one run (the “7B full fine-tune” row in the table above). A team that has measured 40% utilization on its own jobs would get 28 GPU-hours and ~$90; the rule is for before you have measured.

    A realistic project is not one run. The first run finds a data bug, the second a bad learning rate, then two or three are compared, then the one that worked is rerun on the final data: five to ten runs, so $700 to $1,400, before anyone touches a hyperparameter sweep. That is the number to put in the proposal, and it is why the three habits matter more as the model gets bigger.

    The instance

    The model we fine-tune fits on one 24 GB GPU. Single-GPU and multi-GPU SageMaker training instances, same price list:

    Instance GPU GPU memory $/hour
    ml.g4dn.xlarge 1 × T4 16 GB $0.74
    ml.g6.xlarge 1 × L4 24 GB $1.13
    ml.g5.xlarge 1 × A10G 24 GB $1.41
    ml.g6e.xlarge 1 × L40S 48 GB $2.61
    ml.g5.12xlarge 4 × A10G 96 GB $7.09
    ml.p4d.24xlarge 8 × A100 320 GB $25.25
    ml.p5.48xlarge 8 × H100 640 GB $63.30

    Multi-GPU instances are the right tool when the model, its optimizer state and a batch do not fit on one GPU: a full fine-tune of a 7B model, or anything at 70B. They are the wrong tool when the job does fit on one GPU, because the price goes up 5x to 45x and a job too small to split gets no faster. A 3B LoRA run fits with room to spare, so ml.g5.xlarge is the workhorse for this episode. A T4 is too small and too slow for a 3B vision model with page-sized images; ml.g6.xlarge is a fine substitute if g5 capacity is short; ml.g6e.xlarge is roughly 2–3x faster for less than 2x the price, so it becomes cheaper per run once training outweighs the fixed startup (Exercise 2).

    Scaling the same job to more GPUs

    Nothing in this episode is specific to small runs. The training script uses Hugging Face Trainer, which handles multi-GPU data parallelism when SageMaker launches it under torchrun. To run the same script on a multi-GPU instance, change the estimator, not the script:

    instance_type="ml.p4d.24xlarge",                        # 8 x A100, or ml.g5.12xlarge for 4 x A10G
distribution={"torch_distributed": {"enabled": True}},  # one process per GPU, each on a different slice of the data
max_run=6 * 60 * 60,                                     # from the Step 0 estimate, with margin

    Each GPU holds a full copy of the model, so the effective batch becomes batch_size x grad_accum x number of GPUs, and the learning rate usually needs a modest increase. Two lines in the script should be wrapped in if trainer.is_world_process_zero(): so that evaluation and saving run once rather than on every process. When the model, its optimizer state and a batch do not fit on one GPU (a full fine-tune of 7B or more; see the bytes-per-parameter table), data parallelism is not enough: pass fsdp="full_shard" in TrainingArguments (or a DeepSpeed ZeRO config) so the model is sharded across the GPUs, and use instance_count=2 or more for multi-node runs.

    The cost controls do not change with size: estimate GPU-hours from the Step 0 rules, set max_run to about twice that estimate, tag the job, and run a slice of the data on one GPU first so that a bug costs a dollar rather than a few hundred.

    The run

    A training job bills from the moment its instance is ready until the job ends, including the minutes spent pulling the container and downloading data and model weights. In class we train on 120 German-letter pages for 2 epochs and score 15 held-out pages before and after, all inside one job:

    Phase Time Cost
    Startup: container pull, ~130 MB of images, 7.5 GB of model weights (from the shared bucket) ~10 min $0.24
    Score 15 holdout pages with the base model, ~10 s each ~3 min $0.07
    Training: 120 pages × 2 epochs, ~2.5 s per page with gradient checkpointing ~10 min $0.24
    Score the same 15 pages with the fine-tuned model ~3 min $0.07
    One run ~25 min ~$0.60

    Training time scales linearly with pages × epochs, and roughly linearly with image resolution (every 28 × 28 pixel block of the page becomes one token in the model’s sequence). Doubling max_pixels doubles the time; doubling epochs doubles it again. Those two knobs, left at careless values, are why the estimate must be written down before the first run and compared to the real BillableTimeInSeconds after it.

    We set max_run to about twice the estimate. If a run goes past that, SageMaker kills it and we lose at most a dollar, not a weekend.

    The whole episode

    What Instance Time Cost
    Controller notebook (no GPU needed) ml.t3.medium 3 h $0.15
    Mini fine-tune with before/after scoring ml.g5.xlarge ~25 min $0.60
    Exercise 1: same job at 2 megapixels ml.g5.xlarge ~35 min $0.80
    Total ~$1.55

    Compare the classic mistake: doing all of this interactively on a ml.g5.xlarge notebook instance. The class itself costs about the same, but a notebook instance keeps billing after you close the tab. Forgotten over a weekend: $90. Forgotten for a month: $1,029. A training job cannot be forgotten, because it ends.

    Callout

    The three habits

    1. Cap it. Every job gets max_run. Every notebook GPU instance gets stopped when you stand up.
    2. Start small. The first launch of any training script uses a slice of the data and a short cap. The in-class run below is that small first run; the homework scales it up only after it has been seen to work.
    3. Estimate it, then check. Write the number down. After the run, read BillableTimeInSeconds from the job description and compare.

    Setup

    Students never download the data themselves; five things have to be in place before the session. Each is written out in the instructor pages.

    1. Stage the data in the shared read-only bucket from the lesson’s data release (badger-scribe-data-v1, ~130 MB): a few minutes from CloudShell, a laptop or a notebook instance; commands and the read-only bucket policy in Shared data bucket: staging before each term (the same bucket holds the WattBot data for the RAG episodes). The bucket must survive the end-of-workshop cleanup, or be recreated from the release next term.
    2. Stage the base model in the same bucket (badger-scribe/model/churro-3B/, ~7.5 GB, once, from a laptop or notebook instance, not CloudShell). Every job reads the weights from S3 as a model channel instead of 100 students pulling 7.5 GB each from Hugging Face in the same minute.
    3. Run the full fine-tune once (the estimator in the Homework section, all 251 training pages, eval_pages 40) and copy train_summary.json, eval_before.csv and eval_after.csv from its model.tar.gz to badger-scribe/instructor/full-run/ in the shared bucket. Step 3 compares against these. Replace the time estimates in Step 0 with the job’s real BillableTimeInSeconds.
    4. Quotas: ml.g5.xlarge for training job usage at least the class size (request 100). Default is often 0 to 4 and increases take days; file three to four weeks ahead. Full list in Account preparation checklist.
    5. Tell students the bucket name at the start; it is the shared_bucket value in the first code cell.

    Fallback instance if g5 capacity is short: ml.g6.xlarge (L4, 24 GB, $1.13/h).

    This episode runs from a CPU notebook instance (ml.t3.medium or ml.m5.xlarge). The notebook is only a controller: it stages data, launches jobs, and reads results. The GPU lives in the job.

    There is no data upload in this episode. The competition data is published as a release on the lesson repository (three zip files: labels, train images, test images), and your instructor has staged it in a shared read-only bucket:

    • s3://<shared-bucket>/badger-scribe/train.csv, test.csv, metadata.csv, metric.py, sample_submission.csv, transcription_conventions.md
    • s3://<shared-bucket>/badger-scribe/images/<page_id>.jpg: train and test pages together, about 130 MB
    • s3://<shared-bucket>/badger-scribe/model/churro-3B/: a copy of the CHURRO-3B weights (~7.5 GB), so that jobs read them from S3 instead of every student pulling them from Hugging Face at once
    • s3://<shared-bucket>/badger-scribe/instructor/full-run/: the output of a full fine-tune your instructor ran before class, for comparison in Step 3

    The training job reads the images and the model straight from that bucket; the only files your notebook downloads are the small CSVs. Outputs go to your own bucket from the S3 episode, under badger-scribe/.

    Callout

    Working on your own account?

    Download the three assets of the data release and sync them into a bucket of yours under the same badger-scribe/ prefix, then set shared_bucket below to that bucket. From a terminal with the AWS CLI (the notebook instance’s terminal works), one asset at a time so nothing larger than one zip sits on disk:

    BASH 

    %%bash
V=1   # data release version; check the releases page for the latest
R=https://github.com/carpentries-incubator/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/releases/download/badger-scribe-data-v$V
for a in labels images-train images-test; do
  rm -rf /tmp/bs && mkdir -p /tmp/bs
  curl -L -o /tmp/bs/$a.zip $R/badger-scribe-v$V-$a.zip
  unzip -q -o /tmp/bs/$a.zip -d /tmp/bs/badger-scribe && rm /tmp/bs/$a.zip
  aws s3 sync /tmp/bs/badger-scribe/ s3://<your-bucket>/badger-scribe/
  rm -rf /tmp/bs
done

    The jobs below also expect a copy of the base model in the bucket (one 7.5 GB download instead of one per job):

    BASH 

    %%bash
pip install -q huggingface_hub
huggingface-cli download stanford-oval/churro-3B --local-dir /tmp/churro-3B
aws s3 sync /tmp/churro-3B/ s3://<your-bucket>/badger-scribe/model/churro-3B/ && rm -rf /tmp/churro-3B

    The Step 3 comparison against an instructor full run will not apply; run the homework’s full fine-tune yourself instead.
