    Step 1 – Model libraries and safe CSV loading

    PYTHON 

    import torch
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

    PYTHON 

    def smart_read_csv(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Try several encodings when reading a CSV file.

    Some CSVs (especially those with special characters in author names or titles)
    may not be valid UTF-8. This helper rotates through common encodings and raises
    the last error only if all fail.
    """
    encodings = ["utf-8", "latin1", "ISO-8859-1", "cp1252"]
    last_error = None
    for enc in encodings:
        try:
            return pd.read_csv(path, encoding=enc)
        except Exception as e:
            last_error = e
    if last_error is not None:
        raise last_error
    raise RuntimeError(f"Unable to read CSV at {path}")


train_df = smart_read_csv(train_qa_path)
metadata_df = smart_read_csv(metadata_path)

print("train_QA.csv columns:", train_df.columns.tolist())
print("metadata.csv columns:", metadata_df.columns.tolist())
print("\nNumber of training QAs:", len(train_df))
print("Number of metadata rows:", len(metadata_df))

train_df.head(15)

    Step 2 – Load the cached chunks from S3

    In the Bedrock episode we turned every PDF into page-level records, split those pages into overlapping chunks, and uploaded the result to S3 as chunks.jsonl. Chunking is CPU work, so there is no reason to repeat it while a GPU is billing. We download the cached file and load it.

    PYTHON 

    chunks_s3_key = "wattbot/chunks.jsonl"          # in YOUR bucket, written by the Bedrock episode
chunks_jsonl_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "chunks.jsonl")

def load_chunked_docs_jsonl(path):
    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return [json.loads(line) for line in f]

if not os.path.exists(chunks_jsonl_path):
    download_s3_object(bucket_name, chunks_s3_key, chunks_jsonl_path)

chunked_docs = load_chunked_docs_jsonl(chunks_jsonl_path)
print("Chunked docs:", len(chunked_docs))
chunked_docs[0] if chunked_docs else None

    Each chunk keeps a pointer back to its document and page metadata (doc_id, title, url, page_num, page_label, chunk_idx_in_page), which we use later to cite sources.

    Step 3 – Build an embedding matrix

    Now we embed each chunk into a vector using a sentence-transformer model. For WattBot, a strong and relatively efficient choice is:

    thenlper/gte-large (Recommended baseline embedder)

    • Size / parameters: ~335M parameters, roughly 1.3–1.4 GB in BF16/FP16 when loaded on GPU. Fits cleanly on T4 (16 GB), L4, A10G, A10, A100, and all g5.* instances. Offers noticeably better retrieval quality than smaller 100M–150M models without requiring high-end GPU memory. Runs comfortably on g4dn.xlarge, g5.xlarge, or g5.2xlarge during workshops. Lets participants see meaningful improvements from chunking and retrieval methods without excessive compute cost.

    • Intended use: General-purpose retrieval and semantic search across academic PDFs, sustainability reports, and mixed-domain long-form documents. Stronger semantic coherence than gte-base or MiniLM, but still lightweight enough for workshop hardware.

    • Throughput expectations:

      • CPU only: workable for small corpora (<2k chunks) but slow for anything larger.
      • GPU (T4, L4, A10G, A100) with batch sizes around 64–128:
        • 20k–40k chunks/min on L4 or A10G
        • 10k–15k chunks/min on T4
        • 50k+ chunks/min on A100

    We will:

    1. Load the embedding model on GPU if available.
    2. Encode all chunks in batches.
    3. Store the resulting matrix as a torch.Tensor or numpy.ndarray along with the original chunked_docs list.

    Later, we’ll implement a small retrieval helper that does cosine-similarity search over this matrix—no additional indexing library required.

    PYTHON 

    # We'll use a stronger embedding model now that we have a GPU.
# This model has ~335M parameters and benefits from GPU acceleration,
# but is still reasonable to run on a single 24 GB GPU.
embedding_model_id = "thenlper/gte-large"

use_cuda_for_embeddings = torch.cuda.is_available()
print("CUDA available for embeddings:", use_cuda_for_embeddings)

# Single shared embedder object that we can pass around.
embedder = SentenceTransformer(
    embedding_model_id,
    device="cuda" if use_cuda_for_embeddings else "cpu"
)

    PYTHON 

    def embed_texts(embedder, docs, batch_size: int = 32) -> np.ndarray:
    """Embed all chunk texts into a dense matrix of shape (N, D)."""
    texts = [d["text"] for d in docs]
    all_embeddings = []
    start = time.time()
    for i in range(0, len(texts), batch_size):
        batch = texts[i : i + batch_size]
        emb = embedder.encode(
            batch,
            convert_to_numpy=True,
            show_progress_bar=False,
            normalize_embeddings=True,
        )
        all_embeddings.append(emb)
    embeddings = np.vstack(all_embeddings) if all_embeddings else np.zeros((0, 768))
    print(f"Computed embeddings for {len(texts)} chunks in {time.time() - start:.1f}s")
    return embeddings

    PYTHON 

    
chunk_embeddings = embed_texts(embedder, chunked_docs)
chunk_embeddings.shape

    4. Build a simple retrieval step (cosine similarity)

    We are not using a heavy vector database in this episode.

    Instead, we:

    1. Embed each chunk with thenlper/gte-large (done above).
    2. Embed each question.
    3. Compute cosine similarity between the question embedding and all chunk embeddings.
    4. Take the top–k most similar chunks as our retrieved context.

    This keeps the retrieval logic completely transparent for teaching, while still matching the spirit of production systems that use FAISS, Chroma, Weaviate, etc.

    When might FAISS or a vector database be worth exploring?

    For small–to–medium experiments (a few thousand to maybe tens of thousands of chunks), this “plain NumPy + cosine similarity” approach is usually enough. You might consider FAISS or a full vector DB when:

    • Your corpus gets big
      Once you’re in the hundreds of thousands to millions of chunks, brute-force similarity search can become slow and memory-hungry. FAISS and friends provide approximate nearest neighbor search that scales much better.

    • You need low-latency, repeated queries
      If many users (or a web app) will hit your RAG system concurrently, you’ll want:

      • fast indexing,
      • efficient caching, and
      • sub-second query latency.
        Vector DBs are designed for this use case.

    • You need rich filtering or metadata search
      Vector DBs often support:

      • filtering by metadata (e.g., paper = "chung2025", year > 2021),
      • combining keyword + vector search (“hybrid search”),
      • role-based access control and multi-tenant setups.

    • You want to share an index across services
      If multiple notebooks, microservices, or teams need to reuse the same embedding index, a shared FAISS index or hosted vector DB is much easier to manage than passing around .npy files.

    • You need GPU-accelerated or distributed search
      FAISS can use GPUs and sharding to speed up search on very large embedding collections. This is overkill for our teaching demo (and the Wattbot project in general), but very relevant for production-scale systems.

    In this episode we deliberately stick with a simple in-memory index so the retrieval step is easy to inspect and debug. In later episodes (or your own projects), you can swap out the retrieval layer for FAISS or a vector DB without changing the overall RAG architecture: the model still sees “top–k retrieved chunks” as context.

    retrieve_top_k from wattbot_rag.py is that search: normalize the query and the matrix, one matrix multiply for the cosine similarities, argsort for the top k. Open the file to see it; it is a dozen lines. embed_query_with wraps the sentence-transformer as the embed_query(question) callable the rest of the pipeline expects.

    PYTHON 

    embed_query = embed_query_with(embedder)

# Quick sanity check for `retrieve_top_k` on the first training question
first_row = train_df.iloc[0]
test_question = first_row["question"]
print("Sample question:", test_question)

test_retrieved = retrieve_top_k(
    query_embedding=embed_query(test_question),
    chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings,
    chunked_docs=chunked_docs,
    k=3,
)

print(f"Top {len(test_retrieved)} retrieved chunks:")
for r in test_retrieved:
    snippet = r["text"].replace("\n", " ")
    if len(snippet) > 160:
        snippet = snippet[:160] + "..."
    print(f"- score={r['score']:.3f} | doc_id={r['doc_id']} | page={r['page_label']} | snippet={snippet}")

    5. Serve the generator: Qwen3.8-27B in FP8, via vLLM

    For this episode we use Qwen3.8-27B, an open-weight model that Bedrock does not carry, in its FP8 release (Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8), served with vLLM. It is a dense 27B model with a hybrid attention design (most layers use a linear-attention variant with a fixed-size state, so the KV cache stays small even for long prompts), a native 262K context, and a “thinking” mode that is on by default and that we turn off, because WattBot wants a JSON answer, not a reasoning trace.

    Why FP8 weights and not bf16? Inference is not training. No gradients, no optimizer state, nothing is updated, so the only memory that matters is the weights themselves plus the KV cache for the prompt being processed. A 27B model in bf16 is about 54 GB of weights and does not fit a 48 GB GPU; the same weights in 8-bit floating point are about 27 GB, which fits with room for the embedding model and generation. FP8 is near-lossless for a model this size, and it is faster, because decoding is limited by how fast the GPU can read weights from memory. For inference on rented GPUs, reduced-precision weights are the norm (FP8 where the GPU supports it, 4-bit integer where it does not or where memory is tighter); bf16 is what you use when you have memory to spare and a model small enough not to need it.

    Why vLLM and not transformers.pipeline? vLLM is an inference server: it has the kernels for FP8 and for this model’s hybrid attention, batches requests, and manages the KV cache so long prompts do not run out of memory. It is what you would deploy behind an API, and its offline LLM class is a two-line replacement for a transformers.pipeline.

    We will:

    1. Call the model once to propose an answer and supporting evidence.
    2. Call it a second time with a smaller prompt to generate a short explanation (<= 100 characters).

    PYTHON 

    import os
# Keep model weights on the notebook's 100 GB volume rather than the small root disk.
os.environ["HF_HOME"] = "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/hf_cache"

from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

qwen_model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8"

llm = LLM(
    model=qwen_model_id,
    max_model_len=8192,                          # longest prompt + answer we need; the model allows 262K, we do not
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.85,                 # leave ~7 GB for the embedding model and PyTorch overhead
    limit_mm_per_prompt={"image": 0, "video": 0},  # text only: skip reserving memory for the vision encoder
)
print("vLLM engine ready:", qwen_model_id)

    PYTHON 

    !nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv

    The number above is what you are paying for: a 48 GB GPU, most of it now holding model weights and a reserved KV cache. It stays allocated, and billed, until you stop the instance.

    PYTHON 

    def call_qwen_chat(system_prompt: str, user_prompt: str, max_new_tokens: int = 384) -> str:
    """Send a chat prompt to the vLLM engine and return only the generated text."""
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_prompt},
    ]
    params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=max_new_tokens)
    outputs = llm.chat(
        messages,
        sampling_params=params,
        chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False},   # answer directly; no reasoning trace
        use_tqdm=False,
    )
    return outputs[0].outputs[0].text.strip()

print("Generator model and helper loaded.")

    PYTHON 

    
# Quick sanity check for `call_qwen_chat`
test_system_prompt = "You are a concise assistant who answers simple questions clearly."
test_user_prompt = "What is 2 + 2? Answer in one short sentence."

test_response = call_qwen_chat(
    system_prompt=test_system_prompt,
    user_prompt=test_user_prompt,
    max_new_tokens=32,
)
print(f"Generator ({qwen_model_id}) test response: {test_response}")

    6. The prompts

    call_qwen_chat has the signature the shared pipeline expects, generate(system_prompt, user_prompt, max_new_tokens) -> str, and embed_query has the other one. run_single_qa in wattbot_rag.py makes two calls per question with them:

    • The first asks for a JSON object with answer, answer_value (normalized scalar, range or category), answer_unit, ref_id (list of document ids), is_blank and supporting_materials. The retrieved chunks go in the user turn, labelled [doc_id, page N] so the model can cite them, along with the expected answer_unit from train_QA.csv as a hint, so the number comes back in the unit the ground truth uses.
    • The second, made only when the first produced an answer, asks for a short explanation. With with_evidence_type=True it also asks the model to name the main type of evidence (text, table, figure, or a combination) in the strict format evidence_type: explanation, and the code turns that into [evidence_type] explanation for the CSV, so the tag is parsed rather than trusted.

    PYTHON 

    print(ANSWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT)
print("-" * 80)
print(explanation_system_prompt(with_evidence_type=True))

    7. Run over the full WattBot training set

    For every row of train_QA.csv, run_single_qa:

    1. Embeds the question and retrieves the top-k chunks.
    2. Asks Qwen for the answer JSON and parses it (a malformed reply counts as unanswerable).
    3. Decides answerability with a hybrid rule: the question is is_blank if the model said so or the top retrieval cosine score is below retrieval_threshold. Weak retrieval means the model is about to answer from memory instead of the papers, which is what RAG exists to prevent. A lower threshold marks fewer questions unanswerable, a higher one more; change it, rerun, and rescore to see the trade-off.
    4. Copies answer_unit from the row (never guessed), maps each ref_id to its URL via metadata.csv, and makes the explanation call.
    5. Returns one submission-format row; we collect them into train_solutions_qwen.csv.

    PYTHON 

    docid_to_url = build_docid_to_url(metadata_df)

all_results = []
max_N = np.inf   # set to e.g. 5 for a smoke test

for idx, row in train_df.iterrows():
    if idx >= max_N:
        break
    print("#" * 96)
    print(f"QUESTION: {row['question']}")

    res = run_single_qa(
        row=row,
        embed_query=embed_query,
        generate=call_qwen_chat,
        chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings,
        chunked_docs=chunked_docs,
        docid_to_url=docid_to_url,
        top_k=8,
        retrieval_threshold=0.25,
        with_evidence_type=True,
        verbose=True,
    )
    print(f"ANSWER: {res['answer']}")
    print(f"ref_ids: {res['ref_id']}")
    print(f"EXPLANATION: {res['explanation']}")
    all_results.append(res)

solutions_df = pd.DataFrame(all_results)
solutions_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "train_solutions_qwen.csv")
solutions_df.to_csv(solutions_path, index=False)

print(f"Saved solutions for {len(solutions_df)} questions to: {solutions_path}")
solutions_df.head(20)

    Compare answers to ground truth

    WattBot evaluates each prediction using a weighted score that combines three components. Most of the credit (0.75) comes from the answer_value, which must match the ground truth after normalization (numeric answers must be within ±0.1% relative tolerance; categorical values must match exactly). An additional 0.15 comes from ref_id, where partial credit is given based on the Jaccard overlap between your cited document IDs and the ground-truth set. The final 0.10 comes from correctly marking unanswerable questions: if a question is truly unanswerable, you must set answer_value, ref_id, and supporting_materials to is_blank. Any other combination scores zero for this component.

    Component Weight What counts as correct
    answer_value 0.75 Numeric within ±0.1% relative tolerance; categorical exact match; is_blank if unanswerable
    ref_id 0.15 Jaccard overlap with the ground-truth reference set (case-insensitive)
    is_NA 0.10 All required fields set to is_blank when the question is truly unanswerable

    compute_wattbot_score from wattbot_rag.py implements that metric, joins predictions to train_QA.csv on id, and prints the worst-scoring rows. train_QA.csv has no separate “unanswerable” column, so gt_is_na_col="is_blank" derives that flag from answer_value == "is_blank" on both sides. The scorer accepts ref_id either as ;-joined ids (what the pipeline writes) or as the Python-list strings in train_QA.csv.

    PYTHON 

    results_df = compute_wattbot_score(
    train_qa_path=train_qa_path,
    preds_path=solutions_path,
    gt_is_na_col="is_blank",
    pred_is_na_col="is_blank",
    n_examples=10,
)

    Change retrieval_threshold or top_k in the loop above, rerun it, and rescore: with the model loaded, a full pass over the training set takes a few minutes, which is what a GPU notebook is for. Then stop the instance.

    Recap and next steps

    In this episode, we:

    • Pulled the WattBot corpus chunks that the Bedrock episode cached on S3 into our notebook environment, and reused the pipeline code (wattbot_rag.py) from the Bedrock and Processing Jobs episodes unchanged.
    • Created vector embeddings for each chunk and used similarity search to retrieve relevant context for a given question.
    • Used an LLM to generate answers from retrieved context and wrote results out to a CSV for later scoring and analysis.
    • Handled unanswerable questions with an is_blank flag so the system can explicitly say “I don’t know” when the evidence isn’t there.

    This is just a first pass at a RAG pipeline: it works, but there’s a lot of headroom to improve both accuracy and robustness. Some natural next steps:

    • Increase the size/quality of models used for embedding and generation: Try stronger embedding models (e.g., larger sentence-transformers or domain-tuned embeddings) and more capable LLMs for answer generation, especially if you have GPU budget.

    • Add a reranking step: Instead of sending the top-k raw nearest neighbors directly to the LLM, use a cross-encoder or reranker model to re-score those candidates and send only the best ones.

    • Handle figures and tables more carefully: Many key numbers live in tables, figure captions, or plots. Consider:

      • OCR / table-parsing tools (e.g., pytesseract, table extractors, PDF parsers).
      • Multimodal models that can embed or interpret figures and diagrams, not just text.
      • Separate chunking strategies for captions, tables, and main text.

    • Enrich chunks with metadata: Attach metadata like section headings (e.g., Methods, Results), paper ID, year, or paragraph type. You can:

      • Filter or boost chunks by metadata at retrieval time.
      • Use metadata in the prompt so the LLM knows where evidence is coming from.

    • Look for LLMs tuned for scientific literature: Experiment with models that are explicitly trained or finetuned on scientific text (e.g., arXiv / PubMed) so they:

      • Parse equations and technical language more reliably.
      • Are less likely to hallucinate when reading dense scientific prose.

    As you iterate, the goal is to treat this notebook as a baseline RAG “workbench”: you can swap in better models, smarter retrieval strategies, and richer document preprocessing without changing the overall pipeline structure.

    The Processing Jobs episode does the same work, with the same wattbot_rag.py, as short-lived SageMaker jobs, so the GPU only bills while it is embedding or generating. Stop this instance now, and delete it if you are done with the episode.

    Key Points
    • Why self-host at all: Bedrock’s catalog is curated and lags releases; most open-weight models (including Qwen3.8-27B) are not on it. When the model you need is not offered, you rent a GPU and serve it yourself.
    • Inference uses reduced-precision weights: no gradients means the weights are the memory cost. FP8 puts a 27B model on one 48 GB GPU (ml.g6e.xlarge); bf16 would need 54 GB and a multi-GPU instance.
    • The meter never stops on its own: ml.g6e.xlarge is $2.61/h, $167 per forgotten weekend, $1,906 per forgotten month, plus $14/month for the storage volume even when stopped. Stop it when you stand up; delete it when the episode is over.
    • Local-first RAG: For teaching (and small corpora), we avoid an external vector database and instead perform cosine similarity search over in-memory embeddings.
    • Ground-truth units: The answer_unit column is always copied directly from train_QA.csv, never guessed by the LLM.
    • Two-stage LLM use: One call focuses on answering and citing; a second, lighter call produces a short explanation tagged with an evidence type.
    • WattBot conventions: We respect the Kaggle competition format, using is_blank for unanswerable questions and for missing fields.
    • Scalability path: The same logic can later be swapped to FAISS/Chroma and larger models, while preserving the interface used here.

    Content from (Optional) The Same Jobs from the Terminal

    Last updated on 2026-10-19 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 30 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What does the AWS command-line interface (CLI) let me do that the lesson’s notebooks did, and what should I not do with it?
    • How do I see, and stop, everything that is costing money from a terminal?
    • What request does the SageMaker SDK send when I call estimator.fit()?

    Objectives

    • Authenticate the CLI with short-lived Identity Center credentials, never with access keys.
    • List, inspect, and stop training jobs, processing jobs, tuning jobs and notebook instances from the terminal.
    • Launch one training job from its JSON description and recognise it as the request the SDK built in the training episodes.
    • State which resources the lesson never creates from the CLI, and why the account refuses them.

    Optional, self-study episode

    Everything in this lesson went through the SageMaker Python SDK in a notebook. The same account can be used from a terminal with the AWS CLI: to check on a job from another machine, to stop something when no notebook is open, to copy results out of S3 in bulk, or to script a launch. This episode shows the CLI equivalents of what you already did, in four groups: look, stop, copy, launch.

    Callout

    Read this before the first command

    The CLI, the SDK and the console are the same API. Nothing here is more powerful than a notebook cell. The difference is that a terminal shows nothing unless you ask: a notebook instance left running is visible in the console the next day, while an endpoint created from a terminal on a Friday is not noticed until the bill arrives. A past participant of this workshop spent a large share of a year’s credits that way. Three rules apply on the shared account and are worth keeping on your own:

    1. Authenticate with aws sso login only. Never aws configure with an access key ID and secret. Those are long-lived, and they end up in shell histories and committed files.
    2. Launch only jobs (training, processing, tuning), with the same three tags and the same MaxRuntimeInSeconds the notebooks always set. Jobs end on their own. Endpoints, EC2 instances and GPU notebook instances do not, and the lesson never creates them from the CLI, or at all.
    3. An AccessDeniedException on the commands below is intended. The workshop permission set denies endpoint and EC2 creation, instance types outside the lesson’s list, and any job launched without the tags. Do not look for a workaround.

    1. Sign in with Identity Center

    Install AWS CLI v2 if you do not have it, then register the account’s Identity Center once. It asks for the start URL and region of the sign-in page you used in the browser (for the workshop account they are in your sign-in email), opens a browser to approve the device, lets you pick the account and permission set, and asks for a default region (us-east-2 for the workshop account) and a profile name.

    BASH 

    aws configure sso

    From then on, every session starts with a login, and a check that you are who you think you are, in the account you think you are in:

    BASH 

    aws sso login --profile workshop
export AWS_PROFILE=workshop          # PowerShell: $env:AWS_PROFILE="workshop"
aws sts get-caller-identity

    The output names the account ID and an AWSReservedSSO_... role. The credentials expire after a few hours; aws sso login again when a command returns ExpiredToken. Nothing that would still work next month is written anywhere.

    If you are on the notebook instance’s own terminal (JupyterLab, File → New → Terminal), skip this step: the instance’s role is already the identity, which is the reason the lesson works from one.

    2. Look: what is running and what did it cost

    The SageMaker SDK calls you used map one-to-one onto aws sagemaker subcommands. --query is a JMESPath filter that keeps the output to what you asked about.

    BASH 

    # Everything that is running right now, by type. Each list should be short, or empty.
aws sagemaker list-training-jobs   --status-equals InProgress --query 'TrainingJobSummaries[].TrainingJobName'
aws sagemaker list-processing-jobs --status-equals InProgress --query 'ProcessingJobSummaries[].ProcessingJobName'
aws sagemaker list-hyper-parameter-tuning-jobs --status-equals InProgress --query 'HyperParameterTuningJobSummaries[].HyperParameterTuningJobName'
aws sagemaker list-notebook-instances --query 'NotebookInstances[].[NotebookInstanceName,NotebookInstanceStatus,InstanceType]' --output table
aws sagemaker list-endpoints       # must print an empty list on the workshop account

    describe-training-job is the call behind job_cost_report() in the training episodes. The same two numbers are there: training time, and billable time, which includes the startup you paid for.

    BASH 

    JOB=<a training job name from the list above>
aws sagemaker describe-training-job --training-job-name $JOB \
  --query '{status:TrainingJobStatus, instance:ResourceConfig.InstanceType, count:ResourceConfig.InstanceCount, training_s:TrainingTimeInSeconds, billable_s:BillableTimeInSeconds, tags:Tags}'

    Cost is billable seconds × instance count × the hourly rate, exactly as in the notebooks. Tags are returned by a separate call, which is also how you find the untagged job that will show up as “unallocated” on the bill:

    BASH 

    ARN=$(aws sagemaker describe-training-job --training-job-name $JOB --query TrainingJobArn --output text)
aws sagemaker list-tags --resource-arn $ARN --query 'Tags[].[Key,Value]' --output table

    3. Stop: the commands worth memorising

    These are the most useful CLI commands to know. Each one stops a charge.

    BASH 

    aws sagemaker stop-training-job   --training-job-name   <name>
aws sagemaker stop-processing-job --processing-job-name <name>
aws sagemaker stop-hyper-parameter-tuning-job --hyper-parameter-tuning-job-name <name>   # stops every child job
aws sagemaker stop-notebook-instance --notebook-instance-name <name>

    A stopped job keeps its logs and whatever it had already written to S3; a stopped notebook instance keeps /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/. Stopping is never the expensive mistake. Deleting an instance when you are done with it is the step that stops the storage charge too:

    BASH 

    aws sagemaker delete-notebook-instance --notebook-instance-name <name>   # only after it reports Stopped

    4. Copy: S3 in bulk

    The S3 episode uploaded through the console and the SDK. For many files, or for pulling a job’s outputs down to a laptop, the CLI is the better tool:

    BASH 

    aws s3 ls s3://<your-bucket>/ --recursive --human-readable --summarize     # every object, and the bucket's total size
aws s3 sync s3://<your-bucket>/xgboost/ ./xgboost-outputs/                 # download a prefix; only new or changed files move
aws s3 sync ./my-data/ s3://<your-bucket>/my-data/                         # upload a folder the same way
aws s3 rm s3://<your-bucket>/scratch/ --recursive                          # delete a prefix; this one asks no questions

    Downloads to a laptop are a transfer out of AWS ($0.09 per GB). For anything larger than a few hundred megabytes, keep the data in the region and let a job read it, which is the lesson’s pattern.

    5. Launch: one training job, as JSON

    Every estimator.fit() in the training episodes assembled a JSON request and sent it to CreateTrainingJob. Here is that request. Fill in the five placeholders from your notebook: the image URI (run print(xgboost_estimator.training_image_uri()) in the training episode’s notebook), your role ARN (print(role)), your bucket, your tag values, and a job name, which must be unique in the account.

    BASH 

    cat > train-xgboost.json <<'JSON'
{
  "TrainingJobName": "<notebook-instance-name>-cli-xgboost-1",
  "AlgorithmSpecification": {
    "TrainingImage": "<xgboost image URI for your region>",
    "TrainingInputMode": "File"
  },
  "RoleArn": "<execution role ARN>",
  "HyperParameters": { "objective": "binary:logistic", "num_round": "100", "max_depth": "5", "eta": "0.1" },
  "InputDataConfig": [
    {
      "ChannelName": "train",
      "ContentType": "text/csv",
      "DataSource": { "S3DataSource": {
        "S3DataType": "S3Prefix",
        "S3Uri": "s3://<your-bucket>/xgboost/builtin/train_builtin.csv",
        "S3DataDistributionType": "FullyReplicated" } }
    }
  ],
  "OutputDataConfig": { "S3OutputPath": "s3://<your-bucket>/xgboost/cli-output/" },
  "ResourceConfig": { "InstanceType": "ml.m5.large", "InstanceCount": 1, "VolumeSizeInGB": 10 },
  "StoppingCondition": { "MaxRuntimeInSeconds": 1200 },
  "Tags": [
    { "Key": "Project", "Value": "<challenge name>" },
    { "Key": "Name",    "Value": "<your name>" },
    { "Key": "Purpose", "Value": "train_XGBoost_cli" }
  ]
}
JSON
aws sagemaker create-training-job --cli-input-json file://train-xgboost.json

    Three fields to notice. StoppingCondition.MaxRuntimeInSeconds is the max_run you set on every estimator; the SDK would have sent 48 hours if you had not. Tags is the tags= argument, and without it the request is refused on the workshop account. ResourceConfig sets the instance type and count, which determine the cost; nothing in a JSON file prints a price, so check it as carefully as you would in a notebook.

    The CLI returns the moment the request is accepted; nothing waits. To follow the job the way wait=True did:

    BASH 

    aws sagemaker wait training-job-completed-or-stopped --training-job-name <the job name>   # blocks until it ends
aws sagemaker describe-training-job --training-job-name <the job name> --query '{status:TrainingJobStatus, billable_s:BillableTimeInSeconds, failure:FailureReason}'

    Estimate first, compare after, as always: this is the same ~4 minutes billable on ml.m5.large, about a cent.

    Callout

    What the lesson never does from the CLI

    • aws sagemaker create-endpoint / create-endpoint-config: an endpoint is a server that runs until you delete it, with no runtime cap. The lesson serves models with processing jobs and Bedrock so that nothing of this kind exists in the account.
    • aws sagemaker create-notebook-instance with a GPU type: a GPU notebook is $60 a day while you are asleep. The optional GPU-notebook episode creates one through the console, where it stays visible, and deletes it the same hour.
    • aws ec2 run-instances: bare virtual machines have no tags required, no runtime cap and no SageMaker job list to appear in.

    On the workshop account all three are denied by the permission set, as is any instance type outside the lesson’s list and any job without the three tags; the instructor page Account preparation checklist has the policy. On your own account, the same denies take about fifteen minutes to set up.

    Challenge

    Challenge: the Friday-evening check

    You are leaving for the weekend and have a terminal, not a browser. Write the commands you would run, in order, to make sure the account is costing nothing until Monday, and the one command to run if each check finds something. Then run them against your own resources.

    BASH 

    aws sso login --profile workshop && export AWS_PROFILE=workshop
aws sagemaker list-training-jobs   --status-equals InProgress --query 'TrainingJobSummaries[].TrainingJobName'
aws sagemaker list-processing-jobs --status-equals InProgress --query 'ProcessingJobSummaries[].ProcessingJobName'
aws sagemaker list-hyper-parameter-tuning-jobs --status-equals InProgress --query 'HyperParameterTuningJobSummaries[].HyperParameterTuningJobName'
aws sagemaker list-notebook-instances --query 'NotebookInstances[?NotebookInstanceStatus==`InService`].NotebookInstanceName'
aws sagemaker list-endpoints --query 'Endpoints[].EndpointName'

    For anything the first four print: the matching stop-... command from section 3. A job you recognise as yours and expect to finish within its MaxRuntimeInSeconds can be left; a job you do not recognise is a question for its owner, and on a shared account the tags (list-tags) tell you who that is. For an endpoint: aws sagemaker delete-endpoint --endpoint-name <name>, then find out how it was created, because the permission set should have refused it. Buckets cost almost nothing over a weekend and need no action.

    Key Points
    • The CLI, the SDK and the console are one API; the CLI shows you nothing you do not ask for, so its first use is to look and to stop, not to launch.
    • Authenticate with aws sso login and short-lived credentials; never store an access key.
    • list-*, describe-* and stop-* for training, processing and tuning jobs and notebook instances cover almost every reason to open a terminal.
    • A create-training-job JSON is what estimator.fit() sent: the same tags, the same MaxRuntimeInSeconds, the same instance choice, with no price printed next to it.
    • Endpoints, EC2 instances and GPU notebooks are not jobs and do not end; the workshop account denies creating them, and your own account should too.

    Content from Resource Management and Monitoring

    Last updated on 2026-10-19 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 35 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can I monitor and manage AWS resources to avoid unnecessary costs?
    • What steps are necessary to clean up SageMaker and S3 resources after the workshop?
    • What best practices can help with efficient resource utilization?

    Objectives

    • Understand how to shut down SageMaker notebook instances to minimize costs.
    • Learn to clean up S3 storage and terminate unused training jobs.
    • Explore basic resource management strategies and tools for AWS.

    Shutting down notebook instances

    Notebook instances in SageMaker are billed per second, so it’s essential to stop or delete them when they are no longer needed. Earlier in the Notebooks as controllers episode, we discussed using lower-cost instance types like ml.t3.medium (approximately $0.05/hour) for controlling workflows. While this makes open notebooks less costly than larger instances, it’s still a good habit to stop or delete notebooks to avoid unnecessary spending, especially if left idle for long periods.

    1. Navigate to SageMaker in the AWS Console.
    2. In the left-hand menu, click Notebook instances.
    3. Locate your notebook instance and select it.
    4. Choose Stop to shut it down temporarily or Delete to permanently remove it. > Tip: If you plan to reuse the notebook later, stopping it is sufficient. Deleting is recommended if you are finished with the workshop.

    A stopped instance stops the compute charge but keeps its storage volume, which bills at about $0.14 per GB-month. The default 5 GB is cents; the 100 GB volume the optional GPU-notebook episode asks for is $14 a month. If you enlarged the volume to hold model weights, delete the instance once the episode is done.

    Cleaning up S3 storage

    While S3 storage is relatively inexpensive, cleaning up unused buckets and files helps keep costs minimal and your workspace organized.

    1. Navigate to the S3 Console.
    2. Locate the bucket(s) you created for this workshop.
    3. Open the bucket and select any objects (files) you no longer need.
    4. Click Delete to remove the selected objects.
    5. To delete an entire bucket:
      • Empty the bucket by selecting Empty bucket under Bucket actions.
      • Delete the bucket by clicking Delete bucket.

    Reminder: Earlier in the workshop, we set up tags for S3 buckets. Use these tags to filter and identify workshop-related buckets, ensuring that only unnecessary resources are deleted.

    Monitoring and stopping active jobs

    SageMaker charges for training, tuning and Processing jobs while they run, so make sure to terminate unused jobs. Every job in this lesson was launched with a runtime cap (max_run on training and tuning jobs, max_runtime_in_seconds on Processing jobs), so a forgotten job ends on its own.

    1. In the SageMaker Console, go to Training jobs, Hyperparameter tuning jobs, or Processing jobs.
    2. Identify any active jobs that you no longer need.
    3. Select the jobs and click Stop. > Tip: Review the job logs to ensure you’ve saved the results before stopping a job.

    Billing and cost monitoring

    Managing your AWS expenses is vital to staying within budget. Follow these steps to monitor and control costs:

    1. Set up billing alerts:
      • Go to the AWS Billing Dashboard.
      • Navigate to Budgets and create a budget alert to track your spending.
    2. Review usage and costs:
      • Use the AWS Cost Explorer in the Billing Dashboard to view detailed expenses by service, such as SageMaker and S3.
    3. Use tags for cost tracking:
      • Refer to the tags you set up earlier in the workshop. Remember that tags never propagate between resources: your notebook instance, each S3 bucket, each training/tuning/Processing job, and each Bedrock application inference profile carries its own tags, and anything you launched without tags is untraceable after the fact.
      • Tags only appear as filters in Cost Explorer after the tag keys (Name, Project, Purpose) have been activated as cost allocation tags in the Billing console by an account administrator. On UW–Madison accounts this is done centrally for an approved list of keys (KB 72454); on your own account, do it once under Billing and Cost Management → Cost allocation tags. Activation applies only to usage recorded after that point, and new tags can take up to 24 hours to show up. A key that is not on the activated list (a typo, a lowercase project, an extra ModelSize) is silently ignored by the bill.
      • Bedrock application inference profiles cost nothing to keep, but you can delete the ones you created from the Bedrock console or with bedrock.delete_inference_profile(...) once a project is finished.

    End-of-workshop checklist

    Work through this list before you sign off for the last time.

    • Notebook instances: Stop, then Delete (SageMaker → Notebook instances). Includes the optional GPU notebook instance if you created one.
    • Lifecycle configurations: if you created one (for example, a script that auto-stops an idle notebook instance), delete it (SageMaker → Notebook instances → Lifecycle configurations). It costs nothing but is yours to remove.
    • S3 bucket: empty and delete your challenge-lastnamefirstname bucket (S3 → select bucket → Empty, then Delete). Download anything you want to keep first, once: egress is $0.09/GB. Leave the shared data bucket alone; it is the instructors’.
    • Training, tuning and Processing jobs: confirm none are still running (SageMaker → each job list, filter by status InProgress). Completed jobs hold no billable resource; their artifacts are in your bucket and go with it.
    • Bedrock application inference profiles: delete the ones you created (from the Bedrock console, or with bedrock.delete_inference_profile(...) as shown in the RAG on Bedrock episode).
    • GitHub personal access token: revoke it on GitHub (Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens) if you made one for the optional PAT episode.

    Every stop and delete in this list has a one-line CLI equivalent; the optional episode The Same Jobs from the Terminal collects them, for the day you need to stop something from a machine with no browser.

    In the shared workshop account, the instructors sweep the account with aws-nuke after the workshop. That sweep deletes notebook instances and the learner buckets only, so if you forget those, they will still go. It does not touch Bedrock application inference profiles or lifecycle configurations, so those are yours to remove.

    Best practices for resource management

    Efficient resource management can save significant costs and improve your workflows. Below are some best practices:

    • Automate resource cleanup: Use AWS SDK or CLI scripts to automatically shut down instances and clean up S3 buckets when not in use. Learn more about automation with AWS CLI.
    • Schedule resource usage: Schedule instance start and stop times using AWS Lambda. Learn how to schedule tasks with AWS Lambda.
    • Test workflows locally first: Before scaling up experiments in SageMaker, test them locally to minimize cloud usage and costs. Learn about SageMaker local mode.
    • Use cost tracking tools: Explore AWS’s cost allocation tags and budget tracking features. Learn more about cost management in AWS.

    By following these practices and leveraging the additional resources provided, you can optimize your use of AWS while keeping costs under control.

    Challenge

    Challenge: your own cleanup list

    Without looking at the checklist above, list every billable resource you created in this workshop, and for each one write down where it is deleted (which console page, or which command). Then compare with the checklist. Which items would have kept billing if you had only stopped your notebook instance and walked away?

    A complete list for someone who did every episode, including the optional ones:

    Resource Created in Bills while it exists? Where it is deleted
    S3 bucket challenge-lastnamefirstname and everything under its prefixes (docs/, xgboost/, pytorch/, wattbot/, badger-scribe/) S3 episode Yes: storage per GB-month S3 console → Empty bucket → Delete bucket
    Controller notebook instance (ml.t3.medium) Notebooks as controllers Yes while InService; its volume bills while Stopped SageMaker → Notebook instances → Stop → Delete
    Training jobs (XGBoost, PyTorch), tuning jobs, Processing jobs Training, tuning, RAG and fine-tuning episodes Only while running; all capped by max_run / max_runtime_in_seconds SageMaker → job lists → Stop if InProgress; nothing to delete afterwards
    Bedrock application inference profiles RAG on Bedrock No (the calls billed per token when made) Bedrock console or bedrock.delete_inference_profile(...)
    GPU notebook instance (ml.g6e.xlarge, 100 GB volume) Optional GPU-notebook episode Yes: $2.61/h InService, $14/month for the volume when Stopped SageMaker → Notebook instances → Delete
    Lifecycle configuration (if you made one) Any notebook-instance episode No SageMaker → Notebook instances → Lifecycle configurations → Delete
    GitHub personal access token Optional PAT episode No, but it is a credential GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → revoke

    Stopping the controller and walking away leaves the bucket billing for storage, a stopped GPU instance’s volume billing at $0.14/GB-month, and any Processing job that had not hit its max_run yet. Model artifacts in your bucket are the only thing worth keeping; download them once, then delete the bucket.

    Key Points

    • Always stop or delete notebook instances when not in use to avoid charges.

    • Stop any training, tuning or Processing job you no longer need.

    • Lifecycle configurations and Bedrock application inference profiles are not swept by the instructors’ aws-nuke run; remove them yourself.

    • Regularly clean up unused S3 buckets and objects to save on storage costs.

    • Monitor your expenses through the AWS Billing Dashboard and set up alerts.

    • Use tags (set up earlier in the workshop) to track and monitor costs by resource.

    • Following best practices for AWS resource management can significantly reduce costs and improve efficiency.
